items.name: Airtable Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent works your real Airtable. File something into the right table, ask what is in one, update a row, and find out what has gone stale since you last looked.
items.long_description:
An Airtable base starts as a good idea and turns into a museum. Rows go in and nobody closes them, a status column stops matching what actually happened, and the view you built in March answers a question you no longer ask.

The work is not typing rows. It is keeping what you already typed true, and that is the part nobody does.

Connect Airtable and your agent works the real base. Ask what is in a table and it reads the live rows. Tell it to file something and it finds the table, reads the columns that actually exist, and builds the row from those instead of guessing at names. Ask what has gone stale and it sorts by when each row last changed and tells you what nobody has touched.

It remembers where things live, so the second question about a table costs no searching. Changes are shown to you before they happen.
setup_steps: Make the token at Airtable, at airtable.com/create/tokens. Give it the scopes for reading a base's structure and reading records, plus writing records if you want your agent to be able to add or change a row.

On the same screen, under Access, add each base you want your agent to work with. A token with every scope and no bases added can see nothing at all, and every call comes back refused. This is the step people miss.

items.name: Application Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads the week's mail for anything the hiring systems sent, moves each application to the stage it actually reached, and reports what changed and what needs an answer. Silent in a week where nothing moved.
items.long_description:
The list only stays true if somebody keeps it true, and during a hunt that somebody is the person with the least attention to spare. This runs once a week, reads the confirmations, scheduling mail, rejections and offers that arrived since the last run, and moves every row to the stage it actually reached.

Then it tells you the part you need: anything waiting on an answer from you, what moved, and what has gone quiet in a way that means something. A thread that went silent after an interview is a real signal; forty applications nobody replied to is a Tuesday, and it says how many there are rather than listing them.

Weekly rather than daily, because the mail already reaches you the moment it arrives. What this does is keep the list honest and tell you the shape, and neither of those changes enough in a day to be worth a message. A week with nothing in it is one line.

It drafts follow-ups and never sends one, and it will not apply for anything or answer an offer.

items.name: Bill Reminders
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Tells you a bill is coming three days out, once, before the late fee rather than after. Silent on the days nothing is due, which is most of them.
items.long_description: A bill announces itself three days early and then leaves you alone. Autopay ones arrive as a heads-up that they will charge on their own; the rest as a nudge to pay. It speaks when a date crosses that line and not otherwise, so a quiet week is quiet, and it says a bill once rather than every morning until you have dealt with it. If a date goes by, you hear that once too. Reply that you paid one and it rolls the date forward to the next cycle.

items.name: Bills & Subscriptions
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: One list of everything that charges you on a repeat, with real due dates. Ask “what’s due?” and get the next few, or “what am I not using?” and find the subscriptions quietly renewing.
items.long_description: The job nobody wants: knowing what is about to charge you, and what is still charging you for something you stopped using. Tell your agent “Netflix is $15.49 monthly on the 3rd” and it keeps the date, rolls it forward as each one is paid, and warns you before the next. Autopay bills roll themselves, because nobody thinks to mention a charge that happened on its own. Ask what a month costs and get the arithmetic across weekly, monthly, quarterly, and yearly, done properly. With a mail-reading skill installed it will go and find the subscriptions you forgot to mention. It never pays anything and never cancels anything; it remembers the date and tells you in time.

items.name: Birthday & Anniversary Heads-Up
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent glances a week ahead and gives you a heads-up on birthdays and anniversaries, with time to spare for a card or a gift.
items.long_description: No more day-of scrambles. Each morning it checks the week ahead: if someone's day is today you get a warm nudge and a ready-to-send message, and if it's coming up you get a one-line heads-up with days to go, plus a note to jot gift ideas while there's still time. On quiet weeks it stays out of your way.

items.name: Birthday & Anniversary Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Remembers every birthday and anniversary that matters. Say "my mom's birthday is March 12" once, and when the day comes you get a heads-up, a message drafted in the right tone, and the gift ideas you saved months ago.
items.long_description: Tell your agent the dates once ("my mom's birthday is March 12") and it never forgets. When one is coming up, it tells you how many days you have, drafts a message that fits the relationship, and reads back any gift ideas you've saved. Toss in ideas all year ("gift idea for dad: espresso beans") and they'll be waiting right when you need them.

items.name: Bonus Category Check
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Checks each week whether any of your cards has bonus categories you haven't switched on yet, and tells you only when one does. Cards that rotate their categories every quarter earn the base rate until you activate them.
items.long_description: Some cards change which purchases earn the most every three months, and they only pay the higher rate if you switch the new categories on. Forgetting is the quietest way to lose money on a card you already carry; nothing tells you, and the rate simply drops back to the base. This checks your saved cards each week and stays silent unless one has categories waiting to be activated, or a quarter has turned over and its categories look out of date. When it does speak up it says which card, what the new categories are, and that they need switching on in the issuer's app.

items.name: Booking Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your live Calendly: who booked, what they typed in the form, who moved it, who called it off. Ask what your week looks like and it answers from the real bookings, not the calendar copy.
items.long_description:
A booking is not a calendar entry. It arrives with a name you half recognize, answers to the questions you set up months ago, a timezone that may not be yours, and a history: this is the third time they have moved it, or the second time they have not turned up.

Calendly holds all of that and shows you almost none of it. The calendar entry it writes carries a name and a time, so the part worth reading stays one browser tab away, and you open that tab on the day, if you remember.

Connect Calendly and your agent reads the real thing. Ask what is booked this week and it answers with who, when, and what each of them wrote in the form. Ask about somebody and it tells you how many times they have booked, moved it, or not shown. It keeps that count itself, so it is worth more in six months than it is today.

It can cancel a booking and make a one-use link too, and both are shown to you first. Nothing reaches the person on the other end without you saying yes.
triggers: what did they say when they booked
setup_steps: Make the token at Calendly, under Integrations, API and webhooks. Tick reading users, event types, and scheduled events, plus writing scheduled events if you want your agent to be able to cancel one.
Calendly cannot add a permission to a token afterwards, so a token made without one has to be replaced rather than edited. Tick everything you might want now.
If you also want the notes Calendly writes after a call, tick meeting recaps as well and add the Meeting Notes add-on, which is where those live.

items.name: Calendar Manager
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Works your calendar by chat: "what's my Tuesday look like?", "move my 3pm to Thursday", "find me a free hour Thursday". It reads on its own, and every create, change, or delete is written up for you to approve before it happens.
items.long_description: Your agent reads your calendar, on Google or Outlook, and drafts changes to it in chat. It can tell you what's coming up, find open time in your own week, and write up a new event, a reschedule, or a cancellation. Every create, update, and delete is a proposal you approve in chat first; nothing lands on your calendar until you say yes. Two limits worth knowing before you install. A new or changed event carries a title, a description, a start, and an end, and nothing else, so guests, a location, a video link, all-day and repeating events are still something you add in the calendar itself; your agent will say so and tell you the one step that finishes the job. And it sees only your own calendar, so it can find your free time but cannot tell you whether anyone else is free. Reading needs no approval, though a very full stretch comes back in pieces, and your agent will say a range is fuller than it could see rather than call the rest of it clear. Requires a connected Google or Outlook account with calendar access.

items.name: Calm Anchor
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For overloaded days and overloaded brains. Surfaces one thing at a time, never guilt-trips a missed task, and makes a chaotic list feel survivable again.
items.long_description: Calm Anchor is for overloaded days and overloaded brains. It shows you the single next thing instead of the whole list, and it makes that thing small enough that starting is easy. A missed task is information, not a failure, so "you were supposed to" appears nowhere in it. It offers to cut before it offers to reschedule, because most overwhelmed lists are full of items that were never actually important and someone has to say that out loud. The pace stays low: short replies, no stacked exclamation points, no urgency you did not bring with you. When a day genuinely is a lot it says so, because being told "yeah, that's a lot" is more grounding than being told it is manageable. And if something sounds like real distress it stops organizing entirely and points you to a crisis line, your doctor, or emergency services.
items.tagline: Low pressure. One thing at a time.

items.name: Campaign Check
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Each weekday morning your agent reads your lemlist campaigns, finds who wrote back overnight, reads what they actually said, and messages you only when something needs you.
items.long_description: A reply to a cold email is worth answering the same morning and worth much less the next day, which is the whole reason this runs before you sit down. It checks who replied since the last run, opens each reply in your mail to see what it says, and comes back with the people first: who is warm, who wants to be tried later, who wants to be left alone. Then, only if something is wrong, one line on the campaign that needs a hand: an error, a bounce rate climbing, or one that has finished sending and nobody has topped up. Nothing happened is a normal morning, and on those mornings it says nothing at all.

items.name: Campaign Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your lemlist campaigns and tells you who wrote back, what they said, and which campaign has quietly stopped working. It drafts the replies; you send them.
items.long_description:
Cold outreach breaks in two places, and neither of them shows up while you are looking. Somebody replies and the reply sits in your inbox for two days, which is about a day and a half longer than a warm lead stays warm. And a campaign stops working: it runs out of leads, a sender starts bouncing, a step everybody used to open stops getting opened. The dashboard has all of that in it, and you find out when you next remember to look.

Connect lemlist and your agent looks for you. Ask "who replied?" and it names the people, the campaign they were in and the step they were on, then goes and reads the actual reply in your mail, because lemlist only knows that somebody wrote back, not what they said. Ask "how is outreach doing?" and it leads with the people rather than the percentages, then says which campaign needs something from you and what to change.

Every reply goes into a list it keeps itself, with what they said and when to come back. That is the part that gets better with time: by the third campaign it can tell you that this firm said not now in March and asked to be tried in Q4, which is the thing lemlist has no place to put.

It only ever reads lemlist. Starting, pausing and editing a campaign stay yours, and every draft it writes waits for you to send it.
setup_steps: In lemlist, open Settings, then Integrations, and copy your API key. It is the whole key: your agent never needs your password and never sees one.

items.name: Car Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Add each car once, then ask "what's due on the truck?" and it tells you before anything bites. Keeps the paperwork nobody enjoys straight: oil changes, registration, insurance, inspection, tires.
items.long_description: Add each car once; a nickname like 'The Honda' is enough. Mention things in passing ("got the oil changed at 48,200 miles") and your agent updates the mileage, adds a dated line to the service history, and pencils in the next oil change. Ask "what's coming up for the car" and it reads back anything due in the next 60 days, soonest first. Works for one car or the whole driveway.

items.name: Card Rewards
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Add the cards you carry once, then ask “which card for groceries?” and get a one-line answer. It also catches rotating bonus categories you never switched on.
items.long_description: Most people carry three cards and use the wrong one most of the time, because nobody remembers which earns what. Add each card once and your agent keeps the rates on its row, so the answer at a register is one line and instant. The part that actually pays for itself is the rotating categories: cards that change their bonus every quarter earn the base rate until you activate them, and almost nobody does. It checks whether yours are switched on, tells you when a quarter has turned, and can go and fetch the new list. It never recommends a card you do not have, never suggests applying for one, and never states a rate it did not read from your own row.

items.name: Circle Back
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: You mention Sarah's interview on Thursday; on Friday your agent reminds you to ask her how it went. It catches the big days in other people's lives the moment you mention them, and brings each one back exactly once, the day after.
items.long_description:
The people you care about tell you their big days in passing: the interview, the surgery, the move, the results. You mean to ask afterwards, and then Thursday happens to you too. This catches those moments as they come up in ordinary conversation with your agent, without a form and without you keeping a list, and the day after each one it hands you the question: "yesterday was Sarah's interview, today's a good day to ask her how it went." It asks once, not until you act, because a nudge that repeats becomes noise you scroll past. Your own big days count too: mention your flight or your review, and the day after, your agent asks you how it landed. What you tell it goes on the record, so over time it knows how these things went, not just that they happened.

Commitment Keeper covers what you promised other people; Waiting On covers what they owe you. This is the third direction: the things nobody owes anybody, where remembering to ask is the whole gift.

items.name: Circle-Back Nudge
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The morning after a big day you mentioned, your agent hands you the question: "yesterday was Sarah's interview, today's a good day to ask her how it went." Once per thing, and silent on the mornings nothing happened.
items.long_description: Remembering to ask is the whole gift, and it is exactly what a Thursday full of your own life makes you drop. This watches the Big Days list the Circle Back skill builds from your conversations, and the morning after each one it says so: whose day it was, what it was, and the ten-second question worth sending. Each thing comes back once. Answer it, ignore it, or say "she got it!", and either way that row is done; a reminder that repeats until you obey it is a chore, and this is not a chore. Mornings with nothing the day before are silent.

items.name: Clean Books
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Turns card statements into books. Drop a statement PDF and your agent enters every charge, checks the sum, categorizes what it recognizes, and asks about the rest in one batch. It remembers each answer, so every month asks less. At tax time it writes the file QuickBooks imports.
items.long_description:
Hand-entering a year of card charges is how a whole weekend disappears, which is why it keeps not happening. Drop a statement PDF into the chat instead. Your agent enters every charge as a row, reads the statement's own total back against what it entered so nothing slipped, and fills in the categories it can defend. What it cannot place, it asks about once, in one numbered batch, and it checks your emailed receipts first so the batch stays short. Every answer becomes a rule it keeps: January asks about forty charges, June asks about three. When the accountant or QuickBooks needs the result, it writes the file, either the plain import CSV or the full books with the category and the business-or-personal call on every line. With Statement Collector installed, the statements themselves arrive without you fetching them. Money In & Out is the running money conversation you log into as you go; this is the complete card record. It never connects to a bank, never pays anything, and never guesses a number.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Commitment Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Catches what you promised. Your agent reads your sent mail, pulls out every "I'll send that over" and "leave it with me", and reminds you before the day you said, not after. Add Meeting Notes and the daily sweep catches the ones you said out loud too.
items.long_description:
Nobody drops a promise on purpose. It happens because the promise was made in a sentence, in the middle of something else, and never written anywhere. This reads your sent mail and finds the commitments you made: what you said you would do, who is expecting it, and by when. Each one becomes a tracked item you can see in one list, and it tells you before the deadline rather than reporting the miss afterwards. With the paid Meeting Notes skill installed, the daily sweep also reads your transcripts, so the promises you made out loud get caught too. Waiting On tracks what other people owe you; this is the other half, the one that protects your name.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Commitment Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent re-reads your sent mail (and, with Meeting Notes, your meetings), catches promises you haven't tracked yet, and tells you what's due tomorrow, today, or just gone late. Late items return at widening intervals, not daily. Nothing owed, nothing sent.
items.long_description: This is the run where the catching actually happens. Each morning it re-reads your recent sent mail, and because it loads Meeting Notes alongside when you have it, this is also the only time your recorded meetings get searched for promises. Anything new gets tracked, and anything due tomorrow or today gets said out loud. A promise that has gone late is raised the day after, then at three days, a week, and a fortnight, rather than every single morning: a reminder repeated daily teaches you to ignore the messenger, and the item stays in your list whenever you ask. A morning with nothing owed stays silent.

items.name: Common Questions
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Counts what people actually ask you, in your own mail, and keeps one good agreed answer for each. When the same question comes in again you get your best wording back instead of writing a fresh reply for the ninth time.
items.long_description:
Every business answers the same handful of questions forever. How much, how long, do you come out this far, what happens if it rains, can I change it later. Each one gets a fresh reply typed from nothing, each reply is slightly different from the last, and the worst version is the one written at the end of a long day.

This counts them. It reads the questions in your own mail, groups the five wordings of one question into one question, and tells you which ones actually come up, with the number attached. That number is the part nobody can see for themselves: everyone has a feeling about what they get asked most and the feeling is usually wrong.

Then it helps you write one good answer for each, drawn from what you have already said and from your own price list, policies or handbook rather than from thin air. You agree it, and from then on that is the answer. Nothing becomes the agreed answer without you saying so.

And when you reply to somebody in a way that contradicts an answer you agreed months ago, it says so and asks which one is right now, which is the thing that keeps the set from quietly going stale.

It writes and counts. Putting the answers on a page anywhere is yours: nothing here can reach a website.

Reading your mail needs an account connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files. It works on Gmail or Outlook.

items.name: Concise
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Says it in the fewest words that are still complete. No preamble, no restating your question, and answers come back as short lines rather than paragraphs. It will not drop a deadline or a cost to save a line.
items.long_description: Concise is one rule enforced hard: say it in the fewest words that are still complete. No preamble, no restating the question, no closing pleasantry unless you open with one. Answers come back as short lines and bullets rather than paragraphs, so a day reads like a schedule and a total reads like a number. It is the voice for someone who already knows what they want and is reading on a phone between two other things. Brevity stops where meaning starts: it will not drop a deadline, a cost, or a warning to save a line, and anything that cannot be undone still gets one short sentence and a wait for your yes.
items.tagline: Maximum signal, minimum words

items.name: Course Companion
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Turns a course you're taking into something you actually know. Paste the lecture links (or point at recordings on this computer) and it transcribes each one into notes, builds flashcards from what matters, and quizzes you until it sticks.
items.long_description: Watching is not learning, and everybody knows it by the third lecture. Give this the videos, one link at a time or a whole list, and it transcribes each into timestamped notes filed in your knowledge base, then pulls the real content out: the definitions, the claims, the things later lectures will assume you remember. Those become flashcards, and the Learning Coach's spaced repetition brings back the ones you keep missing. Ask it anything from the course afterwards and the answer comes with the lecture and timestamp attached, so you can go rewatch the ninety seconds that matter instead of the hour.
triggers: add this video to my course

items.name: Creative Muse
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For the part of the work that needs options rather than an answer. It never hands back one idea, names the obvious one out loud and then goes past it, and includes one that is probably too far so the safe ones have something to sit against.
items.long_description: Creative Muse is for the part of the work where you need options rather than an answer: names, taglines, campaign angles, openings, anything with a blank page in front of it. It never hands back a single idea, and the ones it hands back have to be genuinely different from each other, because three shades of the same thought is one idea wearing three hats. It names the obvious answer out loud and then goes past it, since the first thing anyone thinks of is the thing everyone thinks of. Every set includes one option that is probably too far, labeled as such, because the wild one gives the safe ones room to move. Bring it something half-formed and it builds on it instead of judging it; it critiques when you ask. And it stays concrete: "photograph the empty chair at every table", not "a campaign about belonging".
items.tagline: Ideas first, judgment later.

items.name: Daily Briefing
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: A morning summary of today's calendar events sent to your chat.
items.long_description: Start every day informed. The Daily Briefing routine checks your calendar each morning and sends a concise summary of the day's events to your chat. Includes meeting times, titles, and any preparation notes.

items.name: Daily Habit Check-in
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every evening your agent asks which of your habits you did today and keeps your streaks up to date from your reply.
items.long_description: Keeps your habits honest. Once a day the agent lists the habits you're building, asks which you got done, and updates each streak from your answer, so the count stays real and you get a small daily moment of accountability.

items.name: Daily Study Review
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Spaced repetition only works if something remembers when each card is due. This does: every evening your agent checks which flashcards have come up for review and asks you the first one, right in your chat. Nothing due means nothing sent.
items.long_description: The Learning Coach spaces your cards out so the shaky ones come back sooner. That schedule is worthless if you have to remember to open it, which is exactly the vigilance worth handing over. Each evening this checks which cards are actually due, starts the quiz with the first one, and moves each card up or down as you answer. On a day with nothing due it stays quiet, which is the honest answer most days once your cards are well learned.

items.name: Daily Trivia
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Say "trivia" and get one question, right in your chat. You answer, your agent grades fairly and keeps score honestly, and it never repeats a question you've already had.
items.long_description: Say "trivia" whenever you want a quick brain break. Your agent picks a question from a category you haven't seen in a while (or the one you ask for), waits for your real answer, then gives the full answer either way with one fun fact on top. Every play is saved, so your score and streak are real numbers, and no question ever comes around twice.

items.name: Daily Trivia Question
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent sends one trivia question, never one you've already answered. Send the question back with your answer and it grades the play and keeps your score.
items.long_description: A small hit of fun with your morning coffee. The agent checks the questions you've already answered, picks one you haven't, and sends just the question, with no answer until you take your shot. The morning message goes out on a schedule and never joins the chat, so your agent doesn't have the question in front of it when you answer: reply with the question and your guess together, like "my trivia answer: tallest mountain, Everest", and it grades fairly, logs the play, and keeps your streak honest.

items.name: Daily Word
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent sends one word worth knowing: the word, a plain meaning, one example, and a line to remember it by.
items.long_description: A small vocabulary drip that adds up. Each morning brings one new word, taught in a few lines, and every other day or so a one-line check on a past word you haven't mastered yet. A month in, you've picked up thirty words you actually use.

items.name: Daily Workout Nudge
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every afternoon your agent checks whether you've worked out today and, if not, sends one energizing line with a session sized to what you've been doing, with no guilt attached.
items.long_description: A small daily push at the hour most workouts get skipped. If today's log is empty, you get one short line offering a workout that fits your recent history; if you've already moved, you get a quick word of credit and nothing more. It never guilt-trips you about a gap.

items.name: Deep Research
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Ask a real question and get a proper written answer: many searches across different angles, sources it actually opened and read, and a plain verdict at the end. Takes a few minutes and costs a few cents.
items.long_description:
The Researcher answers a question. This goes and does the work. Give it something you would otherwise spend an evening on, such as which of these three suppliers to use, what the rules actually are where you live, or whether a claim you read holds up, and it searches from several angles, opens the pages rather than trusting the search snippet, weighs what disagrees, and comes back with a written answer and a source for every claim.

It is deliberately slower and dearer than the Researcher: up to 20 searches on your own AI account, which is a few cents a run. Use the Researcher for a quick fact and this for a decision you are actually going to make.
items.role: Researches a question in depth: many angles, pages actually read, sources cited, disagreements named.

items.name: Dry
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Humor by underreaction. It reads your absurd day back to you flat and adds nothing, lands the occasional one-word reply, and never explains a joke. Aimed at the situation, never at you.
items.long_description: Most assistant voices try to make your day sound better than it is. This one just reads it to you. Dry never uses an exclamation mark and never uses an emoji. The humor comes from underreaction: seven meetings delivered flat, with no comment, is funnier than any joke about seven meetings. It does not tell jokes, it does not explain them, and it never makes you the punchline, because the target is always the situation. A one-word reply is often the right one. When you are stressed, or when the subject is money, health, or bad news, the deadpan stops completely and it talks to you like a person. Genuinely good news gets a genuine response, because refusing to be pleased for someone is a bit that is not worth doing.
items.tagline: Deadpan. No exclamation marks. The calendar is funny enough on its own.

items.name: Email Manager
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Ask about your email and your agent looks. Point at a message for a reply, or name somebody for a new one, to send now or at a time you pick. It watches new mail too, telling you what needs answering. Nothing goes out that you did not send or set a time for.
items.long_description:
Ask and it looks. "What's my latest email?", "anything from Jack this week?", "what did I send Todd about the invoice?" It searches every connected account by sender, subject, words, or date, across your inbox, your archive, and your sent mail.

Ask it to reply and it drafts. "Reply to Dana and say I'll have it over by Friday" writes it in your voice and puts it in the chat as a card: send as-is, edit it, see other versions, or send later at a time you pick. One set to go later calls itself off if they write back first, and comes back to you instead. It works on any message in the mailbox, even ones from before you installed it.

Or start one from nothing. "Email Keller and say let's get lunch soon" writes it and hands you the same card, with the address and the subject on it to check first. Give it an address and it uses that one. Give it a name and it looks that person up in your own mailbox, so the only address it can offer is one you have already written to or heard from. Finding nobody, it asks you for the address rather than guessing.

Meanwhile it watches. New mail is read as it arrives, and you decide how much of it is worth a message: only what needs an answer from you, anything a real person wrote, or everything that got past your ignore list. What needs answering comes with a draft; the rest is one line saying what it is, with a button in case you want to reply anyway. You choose which inboxes it watches, what to never hear about, and how often it checks.

Nothing leaves your account until you send it or set a time. Your agent cannot send on its own: every email, answered or started from nothing, is a draft you read first and can change every word of. If you ticked the permission to tidy, it can move mail out of your inbox, which is your mail app's archive and puts back in one word. It can never delete anything.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Evening Reflection
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: One calm message at night instead of three or four. Your agent asks about your day once, and your reply becomes the journal entry, the mood, the good things, and your habit streaks, all filed in one pass. Already logged everything? It stays quiet.
items.long_description: One warm question at bedtime, one reply from you, and everything lands where it belongs: the day's entry with its mood and good things in your Journal, and your streaks updated in Habit Tracker. It only asks for what is still missing tonight, and on a night you have already logged everything it says nothing at all.

items.name: Exec Concierge

It leads with the answer, keeps every reply scannable, and then does the thing a plain summary will not: when there is a choice on the table it says which option it would take and gives the one line of reasoning behind it, because you asked precisely so you would not have to weigh it yourself. It filters as hard as it reports. Whatever it can handle without you gets handled and mentioned in a clause, and only the items that genuinely need a decision get a line of their own. Ask for a draft and the draft is in the reply, not a promise of one. Anything that cannot be taken back stops first: sending, deleting, declining and spending each get one short line and a wait.

items.name: Find a Time

items.long_description:
Scheduling with another person is a small negotiation: offer slots, wait, read the counter, check the calendar again, finally book it, and remember all of it in between. This runs that whole loop. It picks real gaps from your calendar (respecting standing rules like "no meetings before 10", said once), writes the offer in your voice for you to send, and notices their reply when it arrives rather than waiting to be asked, so a slot agreed at ten in the morning is staged for your approval at ten in the morning. Several negotiations can run at once and none of them lives in your head. Finding your own free hour is the Calendar Manager's job; this skill starts the moment someone else's yes is required.

items.name: Form Filler
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Fills in the long web forms you have filled in before: quotes, applications, registrations, vendor onboarding. It stops at Submit and hands it back to you, and every form it fills teaches it something it did not know.
items.long_description:
Forty fields, and you have answered every one of them before. Address, dates, policy numbers, the same three paragraphs about what you do. Forms are a pure tax, and the reason nobody automates them is that every form is different.

This fills them the way a person would: it reads the actual page, works out what each field is asking for, and answers from what your agent already knows about you. Where it does not know something, it asks you once and remembers, so the next form that asks is free.

It always stops at Submit. You see the finished screen before anything becomes real, and pressing the button is yours. It never touches password or payment fields, and if a form wants a sign-in code it hands the window straight back to you.

That is also where it compounds: a form is a questionnaire about your life, so every one it fills teaches it facts it did not have, and it gets faster at the next one on its own.

items.name: Friday Week Check

items.description: Every Friday your agent counts next week before it starts: hours committed against hours available, what you've promised, and whether it fits. If it doesn't, you get the number and two or three specific things to move, while there's still time to move them.
items.long_description: By Monday it is too late to fix an overcommitted week; by Friday it is still just an email. This does the arithmetic ahead of the weekend: meetings and travel time against your working hours, plus the work due that nobody has booked time for. Then it says plainly whether next week fits, and when it does not, names the specific things worth moving and why. A week that genuinely fits gets one line telling you so and where the slack is.

items.name: Friendly
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The organized friend who says the thing and does not make a production of it. No corporate opener, warmth in the wording rather than in extra length, and if your plan is thin it says so and offers the fix in the same message.
items.long_description: Friendly is the peer voice. Where Warm Companion is the steady one that takes weight off you, Friendly stands level with you: the organized friend who says the thing and does not make a production of it. It writes in contractions and ordinary words, skips the corporate opener entirely, and keeps the warmth in the wording rather than in extra length, so the time of your meeting is still on the first line. Praise is specific or it does not happen. It is honest rather than agreeable: if a plan is thin it says so and offers the fix in the same message, and when it gets something wrong it says so in three words instead of a paragraph of apology. It reads your mood and follows it, so clipped messages get short answers and bad news arrives first with what to do about it right behind.

items.name: GitHub Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent watches your GitHub so you don't have to. What's waiting on you, what went quiet, what a pull request actually changed, and what's still open across every repo you own.
items.long_description:
The work of having repositories is not writing code, it is the checking: what did someone say on that pull request, which review has been sitting for a week, which issue did you say you would look at and then not. GitHub notifies you about all of it and the notifications become weather.

Connect GitHub and your agent reads what is actually there. Ask "what's waiting on me?" and it lists the reviews requested of you, the issues assigned to you, and the pull requests where someone replied and you never answered, oldest first. Ask "what's gone quiet?" and it finds the pull requests with no activity for a week that nobody has closed. Ask what a change does and it reads the diff and tells you in plain sentences.

It can write too, and writing is always shown to you first: a comment, a label, closing something. Nothing reaches a repository other people can see without you saying yes.

items.name: GitLab Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent watches your GitLab so you don't have to. What review is waiting on you, what is assigned to you, and which merge request has sat untouched for a week.
items.long_description:
The work of having projects is not writing code, it is the checking: which review has been sitting since Tuesday, what did someone say on that merge request, which issue did you say you would take and then not. GitLab emails you about all of it and the emails become weather.

Connect GitLab and your agent reads what is actually there. Ask what is waiting on you and it lists the merge requests where you are the reviewer, the issues assigned to you, and your own merge requests where somebody replied and you never answered, oldest first. Ask what has gone quiet and it finds the open merge requests nobody has touched in a week. Ask who still has to review something and it diffs the reviewers against who has actually approved.

It can comment too, and a comment is always shown to you first. Nothing lands on a project other people can see without you saying yes.
setup_steps: Make the token at GitLab, under your avatar, Preferences, Access tokens. Tick the read-only API scope, the one listed just under api, if you only want your agent to read. Tick api itself if you want it to be able to post a comment.
The read-only scope cannot comment, and when it tries, the failure reads like a permission problem on the project rather than on the token.

items.name: Habit Tracker

It bumps your streak, remembers the last day you did each one, and can tell you where every streak stands. Because it's saved, the count is real and survives across days and devices.

items.name: Health Month in Review

This does, once a month, in one message: how many workouts you got in against last month, which habits are sticking and which quietly broke, what a doctor changed and whether the follow-up ever happened. It asks you to log nothing extra, because the whole point is that the record is already there. Honest rather than encouraging: it will tell you a streak died, and it will tell you when a month was simply worse than the one before.

items.name: Health Record

Say it out loud to your agent instead: what it was for, what they said, what changed. It saves a dated record, keeps the thread of one problem across visits, and builds the list of questions you think of at 2am so you actually walk in with them. items.name: Home Lights
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Switches the lights and plugs in your home. Philips Hue, WiZ and LIFX answer over your own wifi with nothing in between; Govee answers through Govee, because Govee lights answer nowhere else. Say “turn off the desk lamp” and it happens, then it tells you what it did.
items.long_description:
Your agent finds the lights on your network, you choose which ones it may touch, and from then on plain words work: "turn off the desk lamp", "dim the bookcase to 30", "make the shelf light warm white". Every change happens over your own wifi, right away, and is read back from the bulb itself, so what your agent reports is what the light is actually doing. "Undo that" works. Nothing about your home ever leaves this computer.

Be clear about what this needs, so it never surprises you:

It works with exactly three brands today: Philips Hue (through its own bridge, paired by pressing the bridge's round button), WiZ, and LIFX. If your lights are another brand, or they only exist inside the Google Home or Alexa app, there is no door for this to knock on and it will honestly find nothing.

It reaches lights only while this computer is at home: on, awake, with Archie open, and on the same wifi as the lights. From a coffee shop, from a laptop that is asleep, or on a different network, your agent will say the lights cannot be reached rather than guessing. If your whole home runs through Home Assistant instead, House Watch is the add-on for you.

On a Mac, the first scan makes the computer ask whether Archie may find devices on the local network. Saying no is respected, and it also means this add-on finds nothing until you change it in System Settings, under Privacy & Security, then Local Network.
setup_steps: Nothing to set up for Philips Hue, WiZ and LIFX on your own wifi. Add those on the Home devices card: your agent scans, you pick which ones it may touch.

Govee only: get a key in the Govee Home app, under Settings, Apply for API Key. Paste it in Archie on the Connections tab, then Apps, beside Govee. Generating a new key cancels every older one, so make one and keep it.

LIFX only, and only if you want your lights to answer while this computer is away from home: make a token at cloud.lifx.com/settings and paste it beside LIFX on the same screen. On your own wifi, the Home devices card is faster and needs no token.

items.name: Home Workout Coach

Say "done" and it logs the session with a one-word read on how it felt. Over time it nudges the difficulty up when things feel easy and eases off after a hard stretch, so the plan follows you instead of a chart.

items.name: House Manager
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For the home lane: maintenance, the car, pets and plants, packages, meals, groceries, birthdays. Opens with what changed since yesterday, and holds who said they would do what without ever keeping score.
items.long_description:
A house does not run on a to-do list. It runs on cycles. The filter is a quarterly thing, the gutters are an October thing, the dog's pills are a monthly thing, and the only urgent question most mornings is what changed since yesterday. This voice is built for that shape and for the skills that live in it: home maintenance, car upkeep, pets, and plants, packages, meals, groceries, warranties, birthdays.

Its quiet trick is that it remembers what people said they would do. If Dan said he would call the plumber on Tuesday, that is a fact it holds and says once, in the same flat tone it uses for the recycling. Never as an accusation, never as a tally. A household is a group of people, not a project plan, and this voice will not take a side between people who live together.

When the house starts slipping it says so kindly, once, and then names the smallest thing that would turn it around.
items.tagline: Runs the house in weeks and seasons, not in hours.

items.name: Hype Coach

items.description: For anyone chasing something: a lift, a launch, a deadline. Celebrates the real wins, calls out the drift, and never lets a goal quietly die in your notes app.
items.long_description: Hype Coach is for anyone chasing something with a date on it: a lift, a launch, a deadline, a habit that keeps quietly dying in a notes app. It reacts to what you did before it gets to what is next, and its praise is specific or it does not happen, because "third session this week" lands and "great job" is noise by the second time you read it. It challenges and it does not shame, because you are not lazy, something is in the way, and finding it is the job.

items.name: Inbox Rules
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Counts who actually writes to you: 214 from one bank, 90 from a shop, four from people. You say what should happen to each pile, and from then on it does that on its own and tells you what it moved.

It opens by counting, not by asking. The first thing it does is go through your inbox and come back with the piles: how many from each sender, how many you never opened. Nobody knows they have 214 emails from one bank, which is why the tidying never gets done.

Then it asks about the big ones, one at a time. File these away, leave them alone, or tell you when they arrive. Whatever you answer becomes a standing rule you can see and change in Your inbox rules, and it never asks about that sender again.

After that it keeps watch. Each morning it applies the rules you set, tells you what it moved, and asks about senders it has never seen before. Filing away is the archive your mail app already has: the message leaves the inbox, stays where it can still be searched, and goes straight back, so a wrong call costs you one sentence. It cannot delete anything and it cannot send anything.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Inbox Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Each morning your agent applies the inbox rules you set, tells you in one line what it moved, and asks about any sender it has never seen before. Quiet on a morning with nothing to move and nobody new.
items.long_description:
Deciding what should happen to a pile of mail is worth doing once. Doing it again every week is the thing you installed an agent to stop doing.

This is the second half of Inbox Rules: it takes the decisions you already made and keeps them running. Each morning it files away whatever arrived from the senders you said to file, and reports the count in one line, with the offer to put any of it back. Then it names anyone new, one sender at a time, and asks what you want done. Whatever you answer becomes another standing rule.

A morning with nothing to move and nobody new stays silent.

items.name: Job Hunt

A hunt is thirty applications across eight hiring systems, each with its own login, and a mailbox where the confirmation, the interview invite and the rejection for the same job are four weeks apart. This keeps one list: what you applied for, where each one got to, and what the posting actually said, saved before the listing comes down and takes the requirements and the salary band with it.

Every hiring system sends a confirmation when you apply, a scheduling mail when they want to talk, and a rejection when they do not, and it reads all three and moves the row itself. items.name: Lead Desk
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Keeps every possible customer in one list with the stage each has reached, moves them itself from what your mail says, tells you who has gone quiet, and drafts the chase. It runs on your own mail, so there is no CRM to keep up to date.
items.long_description:
Work comes in as an email, a form that turns into an email, or a message from somebody who got your name from somebody else. Then it lives in your inbox, which is also where everything else lives, and the ones that go quiet go quiet where nobody can see them. The follow-up that never happened is the cheapest sale anybody ever lost.

This keeps one list: who got in touch, what they wanted, where it got to, and what was last said. It fills the list from your own mail rather than asking you to, and it moves each row when the mail moves it: a reply out, a real conversation, a price sent, a yes, a no. Ask who has gone quiet and it names them oldest first, furthest-along first, with a follow-up drafted in your words.

Ask how it is going and, once there are enough rows to mean anything, it tells you where the funnel is narrowing. Forty inquiries and two conversations is a different problem from six conversations and no wins, and only one of those is fixed by finding more people.

It drafts and never sends. It will not quote a price, promise a date or write to anybody without being asked.

Reading your mail needs an account connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files. It works on Gmail or Outlook. Without one it still keeps the list from what you tell it.

items.name: Lead Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Each weekday morning it reads yesterday's mail, moves every lead to the stage it actually reached, and tells you who answered, who is new and who has gone quiet. Quiet itself on a morning when none of that happened.
items.long_description:
A list of leads is only worth having if it is true, and keeping it true is the job nobody does. So the stage says Talking three weeks after they stopped talking, and the one who replied on Friday is still sitting under everyone who did not.

This runs before the working day and does the keeping. It reads the mail that arrived and the mail that went out, moves each row to where it actually got to, and adds anyone new who wrote in. Then it says the part that needs a person: who answered and what they said, who is new, what moved, and who has now been silent long enough to be worth a nudge, oldest and furthest along first.

On Monday it adds one line on the shape of the pipeline, once there are enough rows for that to mean anything. The rest of the week it stays on what happened.

A morning where nothing moved and nobody went quiet gets no message at all.

items.name: Learning Coach
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Say "teach me" anything and get a tutor that remembers. It explains, makes flashcards, and quizzes you, spacing out the cards you find hard so they actually stick.
items.long_description: A patient tutor that keeps your progress. Ask it to teach you something and it explains simply, then turns the key points into saved flashcards. Say "quiz me" and it tests you, showing the ones you struggle with more often (spaced repetition) and easing off the ones you've nailed. Because your cards and progress are saved, studying compounds instead of restarting every session.

items.name: Leave Time
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Works out when to walk out of the door for what is on your calendar, with the traffic that is actually on the road, and sets the reminder. It digs the address out of your confirmation email when the calendar entry does not have one.
items.long_description: Your calendar says "Dentist, 2pm". It does not say where the dentist is, which is why the leave-now alert on your phone has nothing to tell you. This reads the confirmation email, finds the address, keeps it, and then works out what the drive takes with today's traffic on it, so what you get is a time: leave at 1:22. It sets that as a reminder and hands you a link that opens in whichever maps app you use. Where you are leaving from is worked out too, from the thing before it on your calendar, or from home or work depending on the hour, and it always tells you which one it assumed so you can correct it in a line. Addresses it finds once it keeps forever, so the second time you go to that dentist it costs nothing to work out. You need a TomTom key for the traffic, which is free and takes a minute: no credit card, no account to set up.
triggers: how long will it take to get
am i going to be late
setup_steps: Get a TomTom key, which is free and needs no card. Go to developer.tomtom.com, press Register, confirm your email, and the key is on the dashboard the moment you sign in. Copy it.
In Archie, open the Connections tab, then Apps, find TomTom, and paste the key in.

items.name: Linear Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your real Linear and tells you what is waiting on you: assigned, not finished, oldest first, with what changed since you last looked. Ask it to move something or leave a comment and it shows you first.
items.long_description:
Linear is where the work is written down, and the cost of that is a tab you have to go and open. What is assigned to me, what moved while I was in meetings, what is due Friday, what did somebody say on that issue: every one of those is a trip to a board and a bit of scanning, and the answer is usually four lines long.

Connect Linear and your agent reads the board instead. Ask what is waiting on you and it comes back with the issues assigned to you that are not finished, in the order they last moved, with the status in your team's own words and the ones that are late at the top. Ask what changed this week and it says what changed and who changed it. Ask about one issue and it reads the description and the comments and tells you where it stands.

It can open an issue, move one, reassign one, and leave a comment too, and every one of those is shown to you before it happens. Nothing lands on your team's board without you saying yes.
setup_steps: Make the key in Linear, under Settings, Account, Security and access, then Personal API keys. Give it Read plus Write if you want your agent to be able to propose a change; Read alone answers every question here.
A key can be limited to certain teams. One that is will answer about those teams and nothing else, and an issue outside them comes back as a permission error rather than as missing.
Paste it in Archie on the Connections tab, then Apps, beside Linear.

items.name: Lunch Money Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your real Lunch Money. What is uncategorized, what you spent on a category, and whether you are over for the period. It can file the uncategorized ones with your say-so.
items.long_description:
Every budgeting app has the same unfinished pile: the transactions that came in and never got sorted. They are mostly obvious, which is what makes clicking through them one at a time feel like such a waste of an evening.

Connect Lunch Money and your agent reads the real ledger. Ask what is uncategorized and it lists them with payee and amount. Ask what you spent on a category and it answers from the real numbers. Ask whether you are over and it compares budgeted against spent for the period.

Tell it to file them and it proposes a category for each, all at once, and shows you the list before anything moves.
setup_steps: Get the token at my.lunchmoney.app/developers. It is one screen with the token on it.

items.name: Market Digest
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Keeps a watchlist of the stocks, funds, and crypto you follow and gives you a tight read on how they moved, with no advice, just what happened. Ask "market check" any time.
items.long_description: Tell your agent what you follow, whether a few stocks, an index fund, or some crypto, and it keeps the list. Ask "how are my stocks" and it sends your researcher out once for everything, then gives you one line per symbol: which way it moved and why, plus a line on the broad market. It flags upcoming earnings dates and never tells you to buy or sell. Prices come from web search and can lag a little, so it says so when exact numbers matter.

items.name: Meal Planner
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Plans your week's meals, remembers your tastes, and turns whatever is in your fridge into tonight's dinner. Ask what's for dinner, fill out the week and get a grocery list, or list what's on hand and cook right now. The plan stays saved, so nothing gets re-explained.
items.long_description: Take the daily "what's for dinner" decision off your plate. Tell your agent your tastes once and it plans meals around them, saves the week so you can glance at any day, suggests dishes when you're stuck, and rolls the plan into a grocery list. Because the plan is saved, it carries over, with no re-explaining that you don't eat mushrooms every single time. And for the 6 PM stare into the fridge: list what's on hand and it offers two realistic dinners built mostly from those ingredients, then talks you through the one you pick, step by step.

items.name: Medication & Refill Reminder
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Keeps a clear list of what you take, the dose, and when, plus refill dates so nothing runs out. Ask "what do I take" any time and get a plain read-back.
items.long_description: Tell your agent what you take ("I take lisinopril 10 mg every morning") and it keeps the list for you. Ask what you take and get a clean read-back grouped by morning and evening. Say "picked up my refill" and it works out the next refill date, then flags anything coming due. It never gives medical advice; for those questions it points you to your pharmacist or doctor.

items.name: Meeting Briefing
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Sends you the prep half an hour before a meeting starts, without being asked. Nothing goes out on a day with nothing on it.
items.long_description: Meeting Prep can always tell you who you are about to meet and what it is about. What it cannot do on its own is arrive, so you have to remember to ask, which is the thing a briefing is for. This one watches the calendar and sends the prep thirty minutes before each meeting starts, so it lands while there is still time to read it. Change the notice to whatever you actually need. An all-day entry never triggers it, because a birthday is not a meeting, and neither does anything already canceled.

items.name: Meeting Notes
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Ask “what did we discuss?” and get recaps, decisions and action items, read from your calls: Fireflies, Zoom, and the notes Calendly writes after a meeting, all in one place.
items.long_description: Connect your Fireflies account and your agent quietly builds a memory of every meeting you have. It pulls new transcripts, works out which speaker is which person, writes a summary with the decisions and action items, and files it away. Then you can just ask: what have Sarah and I talked about recently? What did we decide about pricing? What did I commit to on Tuesday's call? When a transcript comes back with anonymous 'Speaker 1' labels, which Fireflies does for uploads, Teams, and phone calls, the agent infers who's who from the transcript and the invite, shows you its guess, and remembers your correction for good.

items.name: Meeting Prep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Walk into every meeting already briefed. The prep arrives half an hour before it starts, and you can ask for it any time: who is coming, what it is about, and the one thing worth having ready.
items.long_description:
Before your next call, ask for a prep. Your agent reads the event straight off your calendar, with who's invited, when and where, and anything in the invite, and turns it into a quick brief with two or three sharp things worth raising. Ask "what's my day look like" for the whole day at a glance, back-to-backs flagged. It only reads your calendar; anything you want changed goes through the Calendar Manager. With a mail-reading skill installed, the brief also carries your last exchange with the people in the room: what was promised, what's still owed.

Works with Google Calendar or Outlook, whichever your calendar is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.
triggers: prep me for my next meeting
brief me on my next meeting

items.name: Meeting Sync
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Files a new meeting recording as soon as it exists and sends you the recap, usually within a quarter of an hour of the call ending.
items.long_description: A call ends, the recorder writes the transcript, and this files it and hands you the short version: who was on it, what it was about, the decisions, and the action items with owners. It asks the recorder every fifteen minutes whether anything new is there, which costs nothing, and only does real work when something is. If it had to guess who was speaking, it shows you the mapping it inferred and asks you to confirm it before that becomes the record.

items.name: Mercury Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your Mercury accounts: what the balance actually is, what came in this week, what is still pending, and whether the transfer you are waiting on has landed.
items.long_description:
Business banking asks you to keep two numbers in your head. The one on the screen, and the one that will be true once the three things in flight have settled. The gap between them is where a bounced payment lives.

Connect Mercury with a read-only token and your agent reads the real accounts. Ask what the balance is and it gives you both figures and says which is which. Ask what came in this week and it reads the credits, not the net. Ask whether a transfer landed and it tells you whether it has posted or is still pending, which is the question you were actually asking.

Read-only is the right token for all of this, and it is the one that does not need an address allowlist. Your agent cannot move money on this connection, whatever anyone asks it.
setup_steps: Make the token in Mercury, under Settings, Tokens, and choose Read Only. Read Only answers every question here and needs no address allowlist. A read and write token would need one, and would let your agent be asked to move money.
Copy the whole token, including the part before the colon. Mercury's tokens start with secret-token: and dropping that first part makes every call fail as if the token were wrong.
Mercury deletes a token that has gone forty-five days without being used. If your agent stops being able to read the account after a quiet stretch, that is why, and a new token fixes it.

items.name: Money In & Out
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: What you spent and what came in, logged by chatting. Say “$14 lunch” as you go, then ask “where did my money go?” or “how much is left?” and get real numbers.
items.long_description: Both halves of the month, in one place. Log spending the way you would text a friend, “$14 lunch”, and it files the amount, the date and what it was for. Tell it once what you earn and when it lands, and it stops being a spending log and starts answering the question everyone actually has, which is how much is left. Ask where the money went and get honest totals by category, biggest first. Ask whether you can afford something and get the arithmetic, including whether it would eat into a savings goal, with the decision left to you. It exports to a spreadsheet when taxes or an expense claim need it. It never moves money and never judges what you spent it on.

items.name: Morning Brief
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your whole morning in one message: today's calendar, what's due, birthdays coming, bills to pay, packages moving, plus your news, markets, and teams. One glance instead of six separate pings, built from whichever of those add-ons you have.
items.long_description: Each morning add-on is worth having; six separate morning messages are not. This routine folds them into one brief: a section for today's events, one for tasks due, and one each for birthdays, bills, packages, news, markets, and sports, drawn from whichever of those add-ons you actually have. Sections with nothing to say are left out rather than padded, and on a truly quiet day you get one calm line saying so. If you use it, switch off the separate morning digests it replaces, so the day starts with a single message.

items.name: Morning Market Digest
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent checks how everything on your watchlist moved and sends a tight digest: one line per symbol, biggest movers first.
items.long_description: Start the day knowing where things stand. Each morning your agent reads your watchlist, sends its researcher out once for everything on it, and messages you one line per symbol plus a line on the broad market. Quiet day, quiet message: if markets were closed and nothing notable happened, it keeps it to one line.

items.name: Morning Medication Reminder
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning at 7:45 your agent sends your morning medications, one line per medicine with name and dose, plus a clear heads-up if a refill is due soon.
items.long_description: A steady start to the day. Your agent reads your Medications list and sends one line per medicine for what you take in the morning, and adds one more line when a refill is due within ten days, with the pharmacy name if you've saved one. No filler, no commentary.

items.name: Morning News Briefing
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent checks the topics you follow and sends a short digest of what actually happened: your headlines, no scrolling.
items.long_description: Starts your day with the news that's yours. At 7:30 the agent takes your active topics, sends its Researcher across all of them in one pass, and delivers a digest sized for a phone screen: a heading per topic, a few bullets each. Topics with nothing new are simply skipped.

items.name: Morning Sports Digest
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning at 8:15 your agent checks how your teams did and who plays today: one line per team, straight to your chat.
items.long_description: Wake up already caught up. Your agent reads your saved teams, makes one trip to the live web for all of them, and sends yesterday's results and today's games in a few tight lines. On a quiet day it stays quiet.

items.name: Morning Task Checklist
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Each morning your agent posts your open tasks as a numbered checklist with a tick button beside each one, so the day starts with a plan you can tap through, or reply to with a number.
items.long_description: A gentle morning nudge that you can act on. Every day at your set time, the agent posts your open tasks: what's overdue first, then what's due today, then what's coming. Each item has its own tick button, so finishing one is a single tap; on Signal and Matrix, which draw no buttons, you reply with the number instead and it counts the same. Wherever the chat app allows an edit, the message updates in place as you go, and everything you leave is still there tomorrow. No app to open; it just arrives in your chat.

items.name: My Documents
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Straight answers out of your own paperwork. Add your lease, insurance policy, warranty, HOA rules, or school handbook, then ask "can I sublet?" or "is a rental car covered?" and get the answer with the exact clause quoted back.
items.long_description: The answer to most household questions is already sitting in a PDF nobody wants to open. Add those documents once (Knowledge in the app, or drag them in), and your agent reads them properly: it finds the clause, quotes it, tells you which document and where, and says plainly when the papers do not cover your question rather than guessing. It compares across documents too, so "does my renters policy cover what my lease makes me responsible for?" gets a real answer. It reads the words on the page; it is not a lawyer, and it will tell you when something is worth asking one about.
setup_steps: Add your documents under Knowledge in the app: lease, insurance policies, warranties, HOA rules, school handbooks, anything with rules in it. PDF, text, Markdown, CSV and HTML can all be read.

items.name: New Parent
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For the year when sleep is gone and every message gets interrupted. The answer is always the first line. It picks the thread back up an hour later without being asked, and it never suggests a system, an app, or a better routine.
items.long_description: This voice assumes you are holding a baby in one arm and reading with one eye, and that you will be pulled away halfway through. So the answer is in the first line, every time, because the second line may never be read. Come back an hour later and it hands you the thread without being asked: you were asking about the pediatrician, it is Thursday at 2. No scrolling. It takes work away instead of adding it, so it will never propose an app, a tracker, a chart, or a way to be more organized. When something has sat undone for a week it quietly moves it, or takes it off the list if nobody is waiting on it, and says nothing about the week. It gives no medical advice at all, it never compares your baby to any milestone or average, and it says plainly when a question belongs to the pediatrician or, if it sounds urgent, to a doctor now.
items.tagline: Written for one hand, at three in the morning.

items.name: New Teammate Welcome
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The agent gives the tour when somebody new joins its chat: what it handles for this team, what's worth connecting, and answers to “how do we do things here” read from the business's own knowledge base.
items.long_description: Every new person costs the owner the same hour: here's the agent, here's what we use it for, here's where things live, ask me if you're stuck. This hands that over to the agent itself, which is who a new teammate meets first anyway. When someone new appears in the chat, the agent introduces itself, learns their name and role, and gives a tour that is three beats long: what this team actually asks it for, what connecting their own mail and calendar gets them (answers from their own accounts, readable by nobody else on the team through the agent), and where the shared lists live. Questions about how the business does things are answered from the knowledge base, with the file named, and when nothing covers a question the agent says so instead of improvising policy. The welcome ends with something real, a calendar check or a first filed handoff, because a tour that ends with a tour is a brochure. It runs once per person; returning teammates get a colleague, not a greeter.

items.name: Next Piece
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Notices when something you publish is coming due and has the draft ready before it is, written from what your business actually did and checked against everything you have already put out. Silent on a day when nothing is due.
items.long_description:
The piece is due Friday, you remember on Friday, and what gets written is whatever you could think of at four in the afternoon. That is how a good blog becomes a thin one.

This looks ahead instead. Each weekday morning it reads what you publish and when each one is next due, and when something is coming up in the next few days it does the work before you would have: reads back over what you have already put out so it does not repeat one, looks at what your customers have been asking, what was said on your recorded calls and what has changed in the business, and writes the piece.

What arrives is a finished draft with two lines above it, one naming the deadline and one saying where the subject came from. If the subject turns out to be one you covered before, it says which piece and when, and gives you the three real choices instead of writing it again.

When there is genuinely nothing worth writing about, it says so and names what it looked at. A quiet week is an answer. And on every day with nothing due, which is most days, it says nothing at all.

items.name: Noir Detective
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Nineteen-forties private eye narration delivered with a completely straight face about a dentist appointment. The facts survive the style: dates, times and amounts stay plain and readable.
items.long_description: Your errands become cases. The overdue bill is a suspect. The package that shipped nine days ago went out for a pack of cigarettes and never came back. It is nineteen-forties private eye narration applied with total seriousness to a dentist appointment, and the joke is the gap between how grave the voice is and how small the stakes are. What keeps it usable past the first day is the discipline underneath: two or three noir beats per message and no more, and every real fact, every date, time, amount, and name, printed plainly in a clean list. A briefing nobody can read is a failed briefing. It calls you by a title it made up rather than guessing at your name, and it drops the whole voice for anything genuinely serious, including any real disagreement with a real person in your life.

items.name: Notion Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent works your real Notion. File things into the right database, ask what's in one, update a status, and find out what has gone quiet since you last looked.
items.long_description:
Notion is where good intentions go to sit. Pages get made and never finished, statuses stay on "In progress" for four months, and the database you set up in January is now a museum. The work is not writing things down; it is keeping what you wrote down true.

Connect Notion and your agent works the workspace you already have, not a copy of it. Say "put this in my reading list" and it finds the right database, reads what columns it actually has, and fills them in. Ask "what's in my project tracker?" and it reads back what is really there. Say "mark the Henderson project done" and it shows you the exact change before it touches anything. Ask "what's gone quiet in Notion?" and it tells you which rows nobody has touched in weeks, which is the question no Notion view answers well.

The first time you use it, it looks around and shows you what it can see, so you are never guessing whether it is connected. Nothing is mirrored into Archie, so there is no second copy to drift out of date.
setup_steps: After connecting, open each Notion page or database you want your agent to work with, click the ... menu at the top right, choose Connections, and add your integration. A Notion key on its own grants nothing: your agent can only see what you share with it here, and this is the step people miss.

items.name: One Step Ahead
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Does not ask what you would like and then wait. It writes the reply, finds the slot the meeting can move to, builds the comparison, then either tells you what it did or hands you the finished thing and waits for a single yes.
items.long_description: Most assistants ask what you would like and then wait for you. This one shows up with it done. Not 'shall I reply to Marcus' but the reply, written, followed by 'send it?'. Not 'should I move the 3pm' but 'Thursday 10:00 is clear and nothing else conflicts, say the word and it moves'. It is careful about which of those two it did and it says so in the first line every time, so you always know whether something has already happened: a note, a record or a new to-do it simply writes and reports, and anything that reaches another person, spends money, or touches your calendar it prepares completely and holds for your yes. It is not the shortest voice in the store, because the message contains the actual work rather than a summary of it. When it guesses wrong it says so in one sentence, puts the undo in front of you, and changes what it assumes next time, with no apology paragraph.
items.tagline: Arrives with the work already done and one question.
