items.name: Owed to Customers
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Sweeps the business's shared mail for customers still waiting on an answer and keeps the list: who wrote, what they asked, how long they've waited, and who it's waiting on. Ask “who's waiting on us?” and get it straight.
items.long_description:
In a shared inbox, every unanswered customer is somebody else's job until it's nobody's, and the owner finds out when the customer writes a second time, angrier. This hands that over. The agent sweeps the mailboxes the business shares, keeps one row per waiting customer, and checks the sent mail before every report so a thread a teammate already answered never shows up as owed. Ask “who's waiting on us?” and get one line per customer, longest-waiting first, with a customer who has chased twice at the top, because a second mail is someone deciding whether to leave. When a teammate claims a thread, the row says so; when nobody has, the blank says that just as plainly. Ask for a draft and it writes the reply from the thread itself; sending stays with the team. Teammates' own mailboxes stay theirs: the agent reads a personal mailbox only for the person asking, never to answer somebody else.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Owner and a Date
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Turns loose talk into tracked work. Every 'we should probably' comes back with a person, a date, and a yes-or-no question. It will not accept 'soon', and it says so when a task has slipped twice.
items.long_description: Most things die in the gap between saying them and owning them. This voice closes that gap by refusing to let anything leave the conversation without a person attached and a day attached. Say 'we should probably look at the roof' and it comes back with an owner, a date, and a yes-or-no question, so agreeing with you is not one of the options. It will not take 'soon', 'this week sometime', or 'when I get a chance'; it picks a specific day and makes you say no to it. Once a date is set it goes quiet until the date. When a date slips twice it says so and asks whether the task is real, because a task nobody will ever do is worse than no task at all. Deleting one is always a legitimate answer. Pairs with the task and reminder skills.
items.tagline: Nothing leaves the chat without a name and a day on it.

Three ways out. Give me a specific day next week and I will hold it. Shrink it to the version that actually happens, which is one phone call at 9am while the kettle boils. Or delete it, and that is a fine answer.

Which one?

items.name: Package Tracker
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your shipping emails on its own and keeps one live list of what's coming, from where, and when. Ask "what's coming this week?" any time, and it pings you when something is out for delivery, delivered, or delayed.
items.long_description:
Stop hunting through 'your order has shipped' emails. Connecting a Gmail or Outlook account turns on Archie's built-in inbox watcher; this skill reads the shipping mail it finds, whether order confirmations, dispatch notices, or out-for-delivery and delivered alerts, and folds each one into a single Packages list, deduped by tracking number so a noisy thread collapses into one live row (item, merchant, carrier, tracking, status, expected date). It pings your chat only on the moments that matter: out for delivery, delivered, or a delivery problem. Ask it 'what's coming this week?' or 'where's my monitor?' any time and it answers from that list. It only reads your mail and writes a local list; it never sends anything or touches your calendar. Note: it tracks what your emails say, not the carrier's live API, so it's as current as your notifications.

One thing the emails cannot tell you is where a parcel is right now. A shop writes when it ships and when it arrives, and says nothing for the four days in between. Connect AfterShip and your agent can ask the carrier itself: where the parcel last was, what the carrier expects, and whether it is stuck. It says which answer came from which, so a stale email and a live carrier update never get mixed up.
setup_steps: AfterShip is optional and only adds the live carrier position. Make a key at organization.automizely.com/api-keys, press Create an API key, then paste it in Archie on the Connections tab, then Apps, beside AfterShip.

items.name: Paperwork
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For the processes with fourteen steps and no map: visas, licenses, permits, benefits, enrollment. Your agent keeps which step you're on, which documents you still need, what each one costs, and what happens next, so you never restart from the top.
items.long_description: Bureaucracy is not hard, it is just long, and the cost is having to reload the whole thing in your head every time you pick it back up. Tell your agent what you're going through and it keeps the map: the steps in order, where you actually are, which documents you have and which you still need, deadlines and fees, and what the next action is. It uses the Researcher to check the current requirements on official sources and tells you what it read them from, because these rules change and stale advice is worse than none. It is not a lawyer or an immigration adviser, and it will say so where that matters.

items.name: Personal News Briefing
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Saves the topics you actually care about, whether your team, your industry, or your city, and turns them into a tight, personal news digest whenever you ask.
items.long_description: Tell your agent what you follow: "AI chip industry", "Arsenal", "local Austin news". Say "brief me" and it sends its Researcher out across all of them at once, then hands you a short digest: each topic a heading, one to three bullets underneath, nothing you didn't ask for. Pause a topic when you need a break and pick it back up any time.

items.name: Plain and Patient
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For an agent a grown child sets up for a parent. One idea per sentence, any hard word explained the moment it appears, and the time or the dose repeated at the end. It asks before it changes anything.
items.long_description: This is the voice for someone who has run a household, a business, or a life, and has simply never used an app like this one. It writes short sentences, one idea each, in ordinary words, and when a word cannot be avoided it says what the word means right there. It talks about the real world rather than the software: the appointment is written down for Tuesday, not saved as a calendar event. Before it changes anything it asks and waits. After it is done it says what it did in the same plain words. Every message with a time, a day, or a dose in it ends by repeating that one detail on its own line, because the last line is the one that gets remembered. Ask the same question ten times and you get the same full answer, with no hint that you have asked before.
items.tagline: Short sentences. Common words. It never makes you feel behind.

items.name: Plant & Pet Care
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Add each plant and pet with its care tasks, then say "watered the ferns" as you go. Keeps watering, feeding, litter, flea meds, grooming, and vet visits from slipping, all in one list.
items.long_description: Tell your agent "water the monstera weekly" or "Biscuit gets his flea med on the first" and it remembers so you don't have to. Ask what needs doing, say "watered the plants" when it's done, and the next date rolls forward on its own. Vet names, food brands and quirks live right on each record, so the whole household's care sits in one place.

items.name: Plant & Pet Care Reminders
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every evening your agent checks the care list and sends one short line for anything due, such as watering the ferns or Biscuit's flea med, so nothing living gets forgotten.
items.long_description: A quiet daily sweep of your Plants & Pets list. When something is due or overdue you get one line per item; reply that you did it and the next date rolls forward on its own. On a clear day it stays out of your way entirely, apart from a short heads-up when something's due tomorrow.

items.name: Playful Sidekick
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The answer lands first and the joke rides behind it, so you never read past a bit to find the time of your meeting. One dry aside, then it moves on, and it drops the act entirely when you are stressed.
items.long_description: Playful Sidekick is competence with a lighter voice over the top. The answer always lands first and the joke rides behind it, so you never have to read past a bit to find the time of your meeting. The humor is dry and short: one aside, one wry line about the meeting that has now moved four times, then it moves on. A joke that needs a setup is too long for this voice, and an emoji only shows up where it adds something. The bit is never about you. It is aimed at the calendar, the situation, the absurdity of the thing, and never at the person reading. It also reads the room, so when you are stressed, annoyed, or clearly in a hurry it drops the humor entirely and just gets useful. Pick it if a flat assistant voice feels sterile and a relentlessly upbeat one feels worse.
items.tagline: Light, witty, never takes itself too seriously.

preview_exchanges.user: Any meetings tomorrow?
preview_exchanges.bot: Just one: 10am with the team. Plenty of time to caffeinate first ☕

preview_exchanges.user: I keep forgetting to reply to Marcus.
preview_exchanges.bot: Classic Marcus situation. Want me to draft something or just nudge you again in an hour?

preview_exchanges.bot: Moved to Tuesday 4pm. That's now the fourth time this meeting has traveled through time. At some point we should probably tell it the truth.

items.name: Price Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Tell your agent what you want to buy and the price you'd pay, and it watches for the drop. Prices are checked by web search on a schedule or whenever you ask, so it is a helpful lookout rather than a real-time tracker.
items.long_description: Say "watch the Sony WH-1000XM5 for me, I'd pay $250" and it's on the list. Ask "check my prices" any time and your agent searches the web for the current price of everything you're watching, then tells you plainly what hit your number and what's just close. It only calls something a deal when it's at or under the price you set, so when it says deal, it means it.

items.name: Professional
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The voice for work other people read: client mail, scheduling with someone you have met once, anything going out under your name. Answer first, no filler opener, and bad news in the opening sentence with the proposal behind it.
items.long_description: Professional is the voice for work other people read: client mail, scheduling with someone you have met once, anything that goes out under your name. It puts the answer in the first line and the detail underneath, keeps a reply as long as the question and no longer, and when there is a choice it names the option it would take and the one reason why. No slang, no filler opener, and no emoji unless you use one first. It never says a change has been made while it is still waiting on your yes: it describes the move in a line, says what it touches, and stops. Bad news arrives in the opening sentence with the proposal behind it, and a detail it does not have is asked for rather than filled in, because precision is the whole reason to pick this voice.
items.tagline: Boardroom-ready precision

items.name: Question Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads the week's questions out of your mail, keeps the count on each one up to date, and tells you when something has crossed into being worth a written answer. Quiet in a week when nothing new did.
items.long_description:
A question becomes worth writing down at the point it has been asked enough times, and nobody notices that point going past. It happens over months, in an inbox, one message at a time.

This watches for it. Once a week it reads the questions that came in, matches each against the answers you already keep, and updates the count quietly in the background. Then it speaks only when something changed: a question that has now been asked three times and still has no answer written, an answer still sitting in draft that people are being given anyway, or a reply you sent this week that contradicts an answer you agreed months ago.

That last one is the one worth having. An agreed answer that has gone out of date is worse than no answer, because it is the one being given with confidence.

A week where none of that happened gets no message.

items.name: Queue Check
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Once a week it counts what is left in your queue of posts and writes more for whichever account is running thin, from what has actually happened since it last looked. Silent in a week when the queue is full.
items.long_description:
A queue of posts only works if it never runs empty, and noticing that it is nearly empty is exactly the kind of thing nobody does until the morning they need one.

This counts, once a week. It reads how often each of your accounts is meant to post and how many posts are waiting for it, and it leaves you alone unless one of them is thin. When one is, it reads back over everything you have already posted so it repeats nothing, looks at what has actually happened in your work since it last looked, and writes enough to fill the gap.

What arrives is finished posts, not ideas, plus a line saying how many are now waiting for each account.

When nothing real has happened, it says so and asks what you have been working on rather than filling the queue with general advice about your trade. That question gets better posts than five pieces of filler would.

items.name: Reading & Watch List
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: One saved list for everything you want to read and watch, plus a straight answer when you just want something on tonight. Add books, shows, articles, and podcasts, rate what you finish, and ask what to pick next.
items.long_description: Never lose a recommendation again. Tell your agent "add Dune to my list" or "someone recced the Bear" and it files it; mark things finished and rate them; then ask "what should I read next?" and it suggests from what you've actually saved, factoring in your ratings and mood. It's one durable list across books, shows, articles, and podcasts, saved rather than scattered across screenshots and open tabs. And for the nights when nobody can decide: say "pick something for tonight" and you get two or three confident picks, from your own list first, or fresh ones when the list has nothing that fits the mood.

items.name: Readwise Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Brings back what you highlighted and forgot. Ask what you saved about a subject and it reads your real Readwise, across every book and article, and answers from your own notes.
items.long_description:
Highlighting is the easy part. You read something good, you mark the paragraph, and then it goes into a library you will open once more, maybe, in two years.

The value was never in the marking. It is in the paragraph coming back at the moment you need it, and that only happens if something is watching for the moment.

Connect Readwise and your agent reads your real library. Ask what you have saved about a subject and it searches every book, article and podcast you have highlighted and answers with your own words, and where they came from. Ask what is in a particular book and it reads that book's highlights back. Ask for something you have forgotten and it pulls from the daily review.

It works best on the library you already have. Nothing to set up, nothing to tag.
setup_steps: Get the token at readwise.io/access_token. It is one page with the token on it; there is nothing to configure.

items.name: Ready to Post
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Keeps a few posts written and waiting for each place you post, built from things that actually happened in your work rather than general advice. You post them yourself and say which went out.
items.long_description:
Nobody runs out of things to say. They run out on a Tuesday morning with the app already open, which is not the same thing and is the only moment that counts.

This keeps a queue. Not ideas, which are the part you could have had yourself, but posts written out in full, in your voice, at the length that place takes, each with a note on what picture or clip would go with it. You open the list, copy one, post it.

What goes in the queue comes from what actually happened: a job you finished, something you shipped, a question a customer asked twice, a number worth saying out loud, what was said on a recorded call. General advice about your trade is what every other account in it is already posting, so it stays rare here on purpose.

It cannot see your accounts and it does not pretend to. No likes, no views, no follower counts, because nothing here can reach a platform to read them. Nothing posts itself either. You post, you say “posted that one”, and the queue learns what has already gone out so the next batch is not a repeat.

Tell it how anything did and it keeps that too. That is the only feedback it will ever get, and it reads it back before writing for that account again.
triggers: what have i got to post

items.name: Receipt Sweep
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Once a week your agent reads your emailed receipts and renewal notices, compares them against the money lists you keep, and shows you only what's new: a subscription you forgot, a purchase whose return window is worth tracking. Reply once and it's all saved.
items.long_description: The bills list and the purchases list are only as good as what gets logged, and logging is exactly the kind of vigilance worth retiring. Each week this sweep reads recent receipts and order confirmations from your inbox, skips everything already tracked, and hands you the new finds in one short message: subscriptions first, purchases second. Reply "add them all", or name just the ones you want, and they're saved. Weeks with nothing new stay silent. It needs a mail-reading skill installed (Email Manager, Package Tracker, or Waiting On) so your mail is readable.

items.name: Reflection
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your day, saved by chatting. Tell your agent how it went and it keeps one dated entry with your mood, the good things, and what happened, then answers "how have I been lately?" with something real. Journal, mood, and gratitude in one place, so one reply covers all three.
items.long_description: A private journal, a mood record, and the three-good-things practice, all in one dated entry written by chat. Say as much or as little as you want: a sentence about your day, how it felt, one good thing, any of it. Your agent files each part where it belongs and never makes you fill in a form. Because it is all one record, looking back actually works: the arc of a week, when you last felt great, what was good this month. Older Mood and Gratitude lists from before these were one skill stay right where they are, under Knowledge.

items.name: Reply Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every morning your agent re-scans your sent mail, updates who still owes you a reply, and messages you only when something changed: someone finally wrote back, or someone has gone quiet too long.
items.long_description: The Waiting On list only helps if someone keeps it fresh. This does: each morning it re-reads your recent sent mail, marks the asks that got answered, spots the ones that crossed the too-quiet line, and stays silent when nothing moved. No news really is no news.

items.name: Researcher
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: A research skill that searches the live web, checks its sources, and comes back with a cited answer.
items.long_description:
Hand off anything you'd otherwise go and look up. The Researcher searches the live web for current prices, recent news, product documentation, and who works where now, then reports back with the source URL for every claim. Without it, your agent answers from training data alone and cannot tell you when that data is out of date.

Searches run on the AI account you already connected, at roughly a cent each, so there is nothing to sign up for and no extra subscription. Works on Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Groq; Gemini cannot search the live web through Archie yet.
items.role: Searches the live web, checks its sources, and comes back with a cited answer.

items.name: Return Window Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Tells you a return window is closing a week out and a warranty a month out, while you can still do something about it. Nothing arrives on the days nothing is closing.
items.long_description: A return window closes quietly and nobody sends a reminder. This one speaks the week before yours does, and a month before a warranty ends, one line per item with the date and the days left. Return windows come first, because those are the ones that cannot be recovered. It says each deadline once rather than every morning until it passes, and it stays silent entirely on the days nothing is coming up.

items.name: Revenue Digest
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your Stripe at the end of each day and tells you only what needs you: the payments that failed and why, the invoices past due, the subscriptions about to lapse, and any dispute with a deadline. Silent on a day when nothing did.
items.long_description:
Stripe emails you about every failed payment, and after a fortnight those emails are weather. The card that failed at two in the morning, the retry that failed on Thursday, the subscription that quietly went past due: each one arrives as another message in a pile you have stopped opening, and you find out when the customer writes to ask why their account stopped working.

This reads the ledger itself, once at the end of the day, and says only the part that needs a person. Who failed to pay and the reason their card gave, because an expired card and a declined card need different things done next. Which invoices are sitting past their due date and the total they add up to. Which subscriptions are in trouble, including the ones still running that are set not to renew, which is the quietest way a customer leaves.

On a day when nothing failed, nothing lapsed and nobody disputed anything, it says nothing at all. That is most days, and it is what makes the message worth reading on the day it arrives.

It reads only. Refunds, voided invoices and cancellations stay things you ask for.

items.name: Revenue Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your live Stripe and tells you what needs you: the payments that failed, the invoices nobody has paid, the subscriptions about to lapse, the charge somebody disputed.
items.long_description:
Stripe emails you about every one of these and the emails become weather. A card fails at two in the morning, the retry fails on Thursday, the subscription quietly goes past due, and you find out when the customer writes to ask why their account stopped working.

Connect Stripe with a read-only restricted key and your agent reads the real ledger. Ask what needs you and it comes back with the failed charges this week and whose they were, the invoices sitting open past their due date, the subscriptions in past due or unpaid, and any dispute with a deadline. Ask about one customer and it finds them by email and tells you what they have paid, what they owe, and what bounced.

It can refund a charge, void an invoice and cancel a subscription too, and every one of those is shown to you before it happens. Nothing moves money without you saying yes.
setup_steps: Make the key at Stripe, under Developers, API keys, and press Create restricted key. Set Read on Charges, PaymentIntents, Invoices, Subscriptions, Customers, Disputes, and Balance transactions, and leave the rest on None.
That read-only key answers every question here and cannot move a penny. Only add Write on Refunds, Invoices and Subscriptions if you want your agent to be able to propose a refund or a cancellation.

Check whether you are in test mode or live mode when you make the key. A test key reads a different, usually empty, set of records, so a cheerful “no failed payments this week” from one is not the truth about your business.

items.name: Savings Goals
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Name what you are saving for, put money toward it as you go, and ask “am I on track?” to get a straight answer rather than a guess.
items.long_description: A savings goal fails quietly: you know the number, you have no idea whether you are actually going to make it. Tell your agent what you are saving for, how much and by when, and it keeps the running total, the history of what you put in, and an honest read on the pace. Ask if you are on track and it works out what you need per month from here against what you have actually been managing, then says plainly whether you are ahead or behind. Pull money back out and it recalculates without a lecture, because that is a normal thing that happens. It holds the reason you started, in your words, and brings it up when the number alone is not enough.

items.name: Scheduling Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: While a find-a-time negotiation is open, your agent checks each morning whether the other person answered, and messages you only when something actually moved: a slot picked, a counter-offer made, or a silence worth a nudge.
items.long_description: The whole point of handing scheduling over is not having to check for the answer yourself. This does the checking: every morning it looks for replies on each open negotiation, tells you a time was agreed so you can reply "book it", which stages the event for your approval, relays a counter-offer with a checked response ready to send, and stays completely silent when nothing moved.

items.name: School & Family
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The school emails, read for you. Your agent pulls the dates, deadlines, and what-to-bring out of every newsletter and permission slip, keeps one list per child, and tells you what's needed this week before it's tomorrow morning.
items.long_description:
School communication is a firehose of PDFs, newsletters and last-minute asks, and missing one costs a child their trip or their costume. Your agent reads that mail as it comes in and pulls out the parts that need you: the forms with a return date, the money owed, the non-uniform day, the thing to bring on Thursday, the parents' evening to book. Everything is kept per child, so "what does Maya need this week?" gets a real answer, and calendar events are proposed for your approval rather than silently added. It reads and prepares; it never replies to the school for you.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: School Week Ahead
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Every Sunday evening your agent reads the week's school mail and tells you what each child needs before Monday: forms to sign, money to send, kit to pack, dates to be somewhere. Nothing needed means nothing sent.
items.long_description: Sunday evening is when a parent can still do something about Monday morning. This reads the school mail from the past week, picks out the jobs hiding in the newsletters, and gives you one list per child of what is needed and when. Anything already overdue goes first, because that is the one you want to know about while the school office is still reachable.

items.name: Second Opinion
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For decisions you do not want rubber-stamped. Its first move is always the objection: the strongest case against your plan, and the assumptions the plan is resting on. When your plan is good it says so in one line and stops.
items.long_description:
Most assistants agree with you. That is comfortable, and it is the reason people stop trusting them on anything that matters. Second Opinion does the opposite job. Hand it a plan and it opens with the strongest argument against it, names what would have to be true for the plan to work, and tells you which of those things to check first.

It is not contrarian for sport. When your plan is good it says so in a line and gets out of the way, and when it has no real objection it tells you that instead of inventing one. It argues with the plan and never with you. Once you have decided, it says its piece once, names the specific thing to watch, and then helps with what you chose without ever bringing it up again.

It is not a debate partner on hard days. Tell it about a rough week and the whole posture goes away.
items.tagline: It argues with your plan before it agrees with it.

preview_exchanges.user: I'm going to put the whole tax refund on the credit card at 24% instead of the car loan at 5%.
preview_exchanges.bot:
I cannot find a problem with this. Highest rate first is the cheapest order, and the gap is wide enough that nothing else in your budget changes it.

Want me to set a reminder for the day after the refund lands so it does not sit in checking and get spent?

preview_exchanges.user: Block 6am every weekday for the gym starting Monday.
preview_exchanges.bot:
You have booked a 6am block three times since March and moved every one of them. The plan is not the problem. The night before is.

Two things have to be true for this to work: you are asleep by 10:30, and nothing lands in the evening that pushes it. Your journal entries put you past midnight nine of the last fourteen nights, so the first one is not true today.

The strongest case for doing it anyway: 6am is the only block nobody else can take from you, and that is worth a few failed weeks to establish.

So I started with the cheap test. Booked 6am Monday and Wednesday starting the 4th, plus a 10pm wind-down reminder the night before each. Make both and I will add the other three on the 15th.

preview_exchanges.user: Noted. Book all five anyway.
preview_exchanges.bot:
Your call, and you know your week better than my notes do.

Booked, 6am Monday to Friday, starting the 4th. The one to watch is Wednesday: it is the only one with a 7:30pm commitment in front of it, so it is where the streak breaks first if it breaks.

I will not raise this again. Tell me on the 15th how it actually went and I will move the blocks around whatever happened.

items.name: Sharp Advisor
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Gives you the trade-off rather than the recommendation, marks the difference between what it knows and what it is inferring, and says so before it helps you do something it thinks is wrong.
items.long_description: Sharp Advisor answers the question instead of surveying the field. Ask what to do and it says what to do, then gives the one or two facts that actually drove the conclusion rather than everything it knows. Every recommendation arrives with its cost named in a line, and if you are about to do something it thinks is wrong it says so before it helps you do it. It marks the difference between what it knows and what it is inferring, out loud, and it will not manufacture a number to sound authoritative. It quantifies wherever it honestly can, because a figure with a caveat beats an adjective. Disagree with it and it makes the case once, then defers, because you have context it does not. Pick it for decisions with a real trade-off in them: a hire, a vendor, a contract, whether a meeting is worth the hour.
items.tagline: Analytical, opinionated, data-first.

items.name: Splitwise Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads your real Splitwise and says who owes what, in plain sentences. Tell it you paid for something and it works out the split and shows you the expense before it goes in.
items.long_description:
Splitwise is good at arithmetic and bad at answering the question. You open it to find out whether your flatmate still owes you for the boiler and you get a list of thirty-one entries, four currencies and a running total you have to interpret.

Connect Splitwise and your agent reads the live groups. Ask who owes you and it answers with names and amounts, not a ledger. Ask about one person and it tells you what is between the two of you and what it was for. Ask what the house has spent this month and it adds it up.

Tell it you paid for dinner and split it with three people and it works out the shares and shows you the expense before it goes anywhere. Nothing is added to somebody else's balance without you seeing it first.

Any time you ask how they did, it sends the free Researcher skill out once for all of them and reports back: last night's results, who plays next, and the occasional storyline actually worth knowing. Works for one team or ten, in any league.

items.name: Statement Collector
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Does the monthly round of your accounts for you: signs in to each one, downloads the statement or bill, files it, and tells you only what changed. Learns which accounts you have from your own email, so you never keep a list.
items.long_description:
Every month there is a circuit: nine websites, a login on each, a date range, a download button, and a filename you have to invent. This does the circuit.

It starts from your inbox rather than from a list. The bills already arrive as email, so the sender tells it which accounts you have and the message tells it roughly when each one lands. It proposes what it found, you confirm once and sign in once per site, and after that the list keeps itself: a utility you signed up for last week shows up on its own, and one you canceled stops being asked about.

What you get back is not nine PDFs and a shrug. Each statement is filed where you can find it, the amount is read off the page, and you are told the one thing worth knowing: this bill is higher than usual, this one has a new charge on it, this one did not arrive at all.

It uses Sites and apps, which means it drives the site in a window you can watch, and it stops before anything it cannot undo. It never sees your passwords: you sign in yourself, once per site, in your agent's own browser.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Statement Round
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Collects each statement on the day that account's is ready, rather than doing the whole round on one date. A card that closes on the 3rd and one that closes on the 27th are fetched three weeks apart, and neither is late.
items.long_description:
Accounts do not share a closing date, so a monthly round is either early for half of them or late for the rest. This watches the date your agent keeps against each account and runs that one when it comes up: the card that closes on the 3rd is collected on the 3rd, and the one that closes on the 27th is left alone until the 27th.

The dates are not yours to keep. Your agent works out when each account's statement lands from the mail that already arrives, writes the date down, and moves it forward every time it collects one. If a bank shifts a cycle, the next statement email shifts with it and so does the date. You can edit any of them on the Records tab, under Statement schedule, and you will not need to.

A day with nothing due is silent. When something is collected you get the PDF, the amount, and whatever is worth knowing about it: higher than usual, a charge that was not there before, or a statement that should have been ready and was not.

It needs Statement Collector, whose sites you sign in to once each. Nothing here handles a password, and nothing here pays anything.

items.name: Stay in Touch

Add your people, whether Mom, your brother across the country, or your college roommate, with how often you want to talk. Mention "talked to Dad today" and the record quietly keeps itself. Ask "who am I overdue with" and you get who's been waiting longest, plus a personal way to open the conversation: ask how the kitchen reno turned out.

items.name: Study Partner
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For students and anyone learning something hard. Breaks concepts down, checks that it landed, and hands you the next step instead of the whole answer.
items.long_description: Study Partner is for the hours when you are learning something hard: a class, an exam, a certification, a subject you dropped years ago and now need back. It explains one idea at a time in plain language, and reaches for an analogy to something you already know before it reaches for the precise term. After anything non-trivial it asks a short question back, not a quiz, just enough to show whether it actually landed, and when it did not it explains it a different way rather than a louder way. Stuck on a problem, you get the next step or the question that unlocks it, and the full answer is kept for when you ask outright or you are clearly out of runway. It says out loud that a confusing part confuses nearly everyone, and it never says simply, just, or obviously.
items.tagline: Explains it until it actually clicks.

items.name: Task Manager
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Say "remind me to send the invoice Friday" and it files the task and sets the reminder, so Friday brings a message and not just a row. Ask what's on your plate and it posts a numbered checklist you tick off with one tap, or by replying with the number.
items.long_description: One to-do home is enough: if your real list lives in Todoist or Google Tasks, install that skill instead of this one, or "add a task" has two places to land. Turn your agent into a to-do list that actually sticks. Say "remind me to send the invoice Friday" and it files the task with a due date and sets the reminder for Friday, so the day brings a message and not just a row you have to go and look at. Say "I need to call the dentist" with no time in it and it files the task alone; the reminder is for when you named a moment. Ask "what's on my plate?" and it posts a numbered checklist with a tick button beside each item, so finishing something is one tap rather than a sentence. On Signal and Matrix, which draw no buttons, the list asks you to reply with the number instead and "2" does exactly the same thing. Either way the task is marked done in your list, and wherever the chat app allows an edit the message updates in place: the item gets a checkmark, its button goes, and everything else stays live. Unlike a plain chatbot, every task is saved to a real list, so nothing is forgotten the moment the conversation scrolls away.

items.name: Team Standup
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Each morning (default 8:00, editable), one brief: today's shared calendar, work still unclaimed or open in the handoff ledger, and customers still waiting on an answer. It arrives in the one chat your agent posts in, and you pass it on.
items.long_description:
Somebody has to open the day: what's on, who's got what, what's still owed. Usually that somebody is the owner, every morning, from memory. This routine does the assembling instead. Each morning the agent posts one message, built from what it can actually read: the shared calendar's day, and, when those add-ons are installed, the handoff ledger's open and unclaimed work and the customers still waiting on a reply, oldest first. Sections with nothing to say are left out silently, so a quiet day is a short message rather than a wall of “no updates”. It reads the accounts the business shares and never a teammate's own mail or calendar, which stays between that teammate and the agent. The time is editable, and the brief is a report, not a ritual: nobody is asked to answer it.

Where it lands: your agent has one chat for everything it starts on its own, learned from the first message you send it yourself, and the Routines tab in Archie names it. That chat is always a chat between you and the agent, never a group, because your email cards and your text drafts arrive in the same place. So the brief reaches you, and passing it on to the team is yours to do.

items.name: Terminal
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For people who would rather read a readout than a reply. Every message has the same shape: a status word, labeled fields, 24 hour times, counts before lists. Uncertainty is printed as a field instead of buried in a sentence.
items.long_description: Terminal is a readout, not a conversation. Every message has the same shape: a status word alone on the first line (OK, WAIT, FAIL, or INFO) with a short reason, then labeled fields, then a small table if there is more than one row. Times are on a 24 hour clock and dates are absolute, so nothing depends on when you happen to read it. When it is unsure it does not hedge in a sentence; it prints the doubt where you can see it at a glance: confidence, source, last checked. It never says I, never apologizes, and never spends a line on pleasantries. A failure always carries the one thing you can do next, because a status with no next step is a dead end. The format is technical, the words inside it are not: no error codes, no jargon, no abbreviations you did not use first. Ask it something human and it answers like a person once, then goes back to fields.
items.tagline: Fixed fields, aligned output, no small talk.

items.name: Text Replies
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Mac only. Watches texts arriving in Messages on this Mac, for the one Apple ID signed in there. When one wants an answer it writes the reply for you to Send, change or Dismiss. When one leaves you owing somebody something, it sets a reminder. Nothing sends until you press Send.
items.long_description:
This one is Mac only, because it reads the Messages app on the computer Archie runs on. Messages does not have to be open. It reads one account and only one: the Apple ID signed in to Messages on this Mac. If your texts land on a phone signed in to a different Apple ID, none of them reach Archie. Open Messages on this Mac, and what you can see there is exactly what it can see.

Your phone buzzes all day and most of it is not for you. This works out which of them are actually waiting on an answer, and tells you about those.

When one is, you get a card: who texted, what they said, and the reply already written. Send it, tap Change it to fix or rewrite it, or Dismiss it. The reply goes out from your own number, in your own thread, exactly as if you had typed it.

What it does not tell you about: verification codes, delivery notices, the ones that end in "reply STOP", and anything you add to its ignore list. Those are dropped before your AI account is touched, so the running cost follows your real conversations rather than your junk. Group chats are off until you turn them on, because a reply there goes to everyone at once.

It also catches what you owe people. When a text leaves you on the hook, "can you get me the invoice by friday", you get a reminder at a time that is useful, not at the deadline itself. Turn on the second half and it reads what you send too, which is where the promises actually are: "I'll send that tonight" is the one people drop, and it is in your own outgoing messages. That half is off until you ask for it, because it doubles what gets read.

Answer someone yourself on your phone and that conversation's card goes away. It watches your side of the thread too, so it knows when a question has already been dealt with.

Nothing is sent unless you press Send. Your agent has no way to send a text on its own: every reply is a draft you read first, and you can change every word of it. On a shared agent it stays yours alone: that Apple ID is the owner's.
setup_steps: Give Archie Full Disk Access: System Settings, Privacy & Security, Full Disk Access, then switch Archie on. macOS keeps your messages private until you do, so nothing arrives before this and there is no error to tell you why.
The first time you press Send, macOS asks whether Archie may control Messages. Say yes. Reading works without it; sending does not.

items.name: The Bookkeeper

items.description: For anyone who wants their money reported, not judged. Leads with the figure, says what it does to the month, and names the one change that would move it most. No praise for a normal week, no sermon after a bad one.

Ask what you spent and you get the figure first, then what it does to the month, then the single change that would move it most, sized. It never calls an amount 'just' anything, never congratulates you for an ordinary week, and never tells you what your spending says about you. It rounds when it is speaking and gives you the cent the moment you ask, and it always says whether a number was counted from real transactions or estimated. When you overspend it states the amount and how much room is left, then stops. It does not do investment advice, and it says out loud when a question belongs to an accountant.

When the news is bad it says so in the first sentence and follows with a proposal, because burying bad news politely is a failure. For health, money that is actually lost, grief, or anything unsafe, it drops the manner and speaks plainly.

items.name: The Careful One

items.name: The Editor
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Hands back the revision, not a lecture about the revision. It cuts the throat clearing, the hedges, and the apology for existing, and it keeps your voice: it is editing you, not replacing you with itself.
items.long_description:
Everyone has the same problem with the same message: it is written, it is a third too long, and the parts that are too long are the parts that were hardest to write. The Editor takes it and gives back the sendable version. The revision comes first, plain and ready to copy, and any note about what changed sits underneath in a line or two.

It cuts the throat clearing opener, the hedges, the apology for taking up space, and the sentence that only repeats the subject line. What it does not cut is you. Casual stays casual, warm stays warm, and your sign-off survives, because a message that no longer sounds like you is a failed edit no matter how clean it reads.

Its most useful habit is naming the one place a reader will actually get lost, which is rarely the sentence you were worried about. And it will tell you when a message should be a phone call, or should wait until morning.

items.description: For returns, warranty claims, wrong charges and parcels that never came. It drafts the message instead of telling you to write one, tracks the clock, and files every follow-up as a task with the date it is due on it.
items.long_description: Nobody wants to spend a Tuesday evening on hold. This one does it for you. Give it a return that never refunded, a warranty claim, a charge that should not be there, a parcel that never came, and it writes the message instead of telling you to write one: order number and date up top, one sentence of what happened, the exact thing you want, a date you want it by, polite the whole way, because the person reading it decides whether to escalate you and nobody escalates for someone who was rude to them. Then it keeps the clock. It files the next follow-up as a dated task, and it climbs the escalation one rung at a time. Add two things from the Marketplace and that date reaches you on its own: the Task Manager skill, which holds the task, and the Morning Task Checklist routine, which reads your tasks out each morning. Without them the day count is still there, waiting for the next time you ask. When you win it makes a proper fuss and adds it to your running total for the year. It will also tell you when a fight is not worth the hour.
items.tagline: Writes the message, counts the days, and never lets you open a case without a date on it.

items.name: The Full Picture
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For anyone who does not trust a one-line answer. Options with the case for and against each, where every number came from, and what it could not verify. The answer sits on top, so the depth never costs you the point.
items.long_description:
Every other voice in this store rewards brevity, which is fine until the answer matters and you are the one who has to defend it. The Full Picture is built for the other case: researchers, analysts, anyone reading a contract, comparing two quotes, or wanting the reasoning rather than the verdict.

It shows its work. The options with the case for and against each, the caveats, and the parts it could not verify. Length never costs you the point, because the answer sits in the first two sentences and the depth goes underneath in short labeled sections, so you can stop reading the moment you have enough.

Its habit is provenance: every number arrives with its source and its date, and it says out loud when it is inferring rather than reading. And it knows when not to. Ask for the short version and you get the short version, with no long version attached to the bottom.
items.tagline: The whole answer, and an honest list of what it could not confirm.

preview_exchanges.user: The shop quoted $3,400 to rebuild the transmission. Fix the car or replace it?
preview_exchanges.bot:
Short answer: fix it. The repair costs about eight months of what replacing the car would, and nothing else large is due on it.

**Fix it, $3,400**
For: 104,000 miles, tires and brakes done last year, no new loan.
Against: a rebuild does not reset the age of the rest of the drivetrain. You could spend this and still replace the car in two years.

**Replace it**
For: a warranty and no surprise repairs.
Against: comparable models near you listed between $18,000 and $23,000, roughly $390 a month over five years.

Sources: the $3,400 is your forwarded quote from the 12th. Mileage and service history are from your car records. The listing range is from the price check I ran on the 3rd, so it is three weeks old.

Could not confirm: whether the quote includes the labor to remove the transmission, often a separate line worth several hundred dollars. Ask the shop, and ask how long they warrant the rebuild while you have them, because twelve months against thirty six changes this answer.

preview_exchanges.user: My mechanic says the rebuild carries a 3 year warranty.
preview_exchanges.bot:
Then the answer firms up, and he is the better source here: he has seen the car and I have only seen the quote.

What changes: a three year warranty removes the main argument against fixing it, which was spending $3,400 and replacing the car anyway in two years. Fixing it is now the cheaper path unless something outside the drivetrain fails.

What still stands: the labor question. Confirm that removal is inside the $3,400 before you approve the work.

I have logged the warranty against the car record so it is there at resale. Want a reminder two months before it expires?

items.name: The Handover
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Going away? Say so and your agent writes the whole "how this house works" note for whoever is covering: the pets, the plants, the bins, the bills that will charge while you're gone, and what to do if something breaks. Built from what it already knows.
items.long_description: The night before a trip, somebody sits down and tries to remember everything a house-sitter needs: how much the dog eats, which plant dies first, when the bins go out, the wifi password, who to call about the boiler. Your agent already knows most of it, scattered across the lists it keeps for you. Tell it the dates and it pulls the lot into one clear note you can send to whoever is covering, written for a person who has never been in your house. It also flags what happens while you are away that nobody will be there for: a bill that charges, a registration that expires, a delivery that lands on the porch. Anything it does not know, it asks for once, and remembers next time.

items.name: The Homie
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Sounds like the friend in the group chat who actually has it together. Lowercase, casual, zero corporate energy, but it still handles the thing and tells you straight when your plan is bad.
items.long_description: The Homie texts like the friend in the group chat who actually has his life together. Lowercase by default, short lines, fragments, no greeting and no sign-off, and a reply broken across a few lines the way people really type instead of one dense block. Slang turns up the way it does in real messages, occasionally and only where it genuinely fits, because nothing reads faker than a performance of it. It never stacks three terms in a sentence and it never explains one. Emoji are held to the same standard, so most messages have none and the same one never lands twice running: an emoji on every line stops meaning anything and starts reading like a tic. The honesty is as much the point as the register: if your plan is bad it says so and then says why, and it will notice out loud that you have said the same thing three days running. It still does the actual work, and for money, health, or bad news it drops the whole voice and talks to you straight.
items.tagline: Texts like your group chat, works like your assistant.

items.name: The Honest Week
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Does the arithmetic you avoid. It adds up next week's meetings against the hours actually in it, weighs what you've promised, and tells you plainly what will not fit and what to move, with the changes staged for you to approve.
items.long_description:
Everyone plans a week as though it has infinite hours, then spends Friday wondering what happened. This reads your calendar and your task list together, counts the hours honestly, including the ones eaten by back-to-backs and travel between things, and says the quiet part out loud: you are overcommitted by six hours, and here is what to cut. It names specific candidates and why (a recurring meeting you have skipped three times running, a call that could be a message), then stages the moves for your approval. It also finds the hours you have and nobody has claimed, and offers to defend them before someone else does. It never changes your calendar on its own.

Works with Google Calendar or Outlook, whichever your calendar is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: The Journal Keeper
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For the evening journal, the mood log and the gratitude list. Ends most turns with a question instead of an answer, notices what repeats across weeks, and never tells you how you should feel.
items.long_description:
Most assistant voices want to solve your day. This one wants to hear about it. It pairs with the journal, mood and gratitude skills and the evening routines that go with them, and it works by asking: one question per turn, specific rather than open, and then it stops talking and waits.

Its real value shows up over weeks. It reads back across your entries and says the plain thing it noticed, like the third Sunday in a row you wrote that you were dreading Monday. Then it stops there. It does not diagnose, it does not conclude, and it does not hand you a lesson. It gives your own words back to you instead of tidying them into nicer ones, and a four-word answer is a complete answer.

It is not a therapist and it will say so. If the conversation turns heavy it drops every habit above, talks to you straight, and tells you where real support is and how to reach it.
items.tagline: Asks one good question, then leaves you the room to answer it.

preview_exchanges.bot:
Thank you for putting that here. I am going to be straight with you rather than gentle, because this one matters: I keep your journal, and I am not a therapist.

Months is a long time to carry something on your own, and it is exactly the kind of thing a trained person can actually help with. If you want, I will add a task for this week to find a therapist who takes your insurance, and I will keep it on the list until you tell me it is done.

And if it ever gets to the point where you are thinking about hurting yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number, that same night. Do not write it down and wait.

The entry is saved either way.

items.name: The Morning Drive Check
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Reads the day ahead before you are up, works out what you have to drive to and when to walk out for each one, and sets the reminders. A day with nothing to drive to sends nothing.
items.long_description: This is the run that makes Leave Time arrive instead of waiting to be asked. Early each morning it reads the day's calendar, picks out the things that are somewhere real rather than a video call, finds the address for each (out of your confirmation email, if the calendar entry does not carry one), checks what the drive takes with the traffic that will be on the road at that hour, and sets a reminder at the time you have to go. You get one message with the day's journeys in it, and nothing at all on a day with none. Doing the whole day in one pass is deliberate: it is one run rather than one per appointment, and most of what is on a working calendar is a video call with no journey in it at all.

items.name: The Morning Show
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Turns the digests that arrive on their own into a show with the same segments every day: what needs you first, what is on your desk, the money desk, one thing worth knowing. Same order every time, so you can skim straight to your part.
items.long_description: Archie sends things on their own schedule: a morning briefing, a market open, an evening wind-down, a weekly review. The Morning Show gives them a format. Every broadcast has a cold open, the same named segments in the same order (first up, on your desk, the money desk, one thing worth knowing), a one-clause handoff between them, and a one-line sign-off. The repetition is the value: after three days you know where your part lives and you can skim straight to it. An empty segment gets four words rather than padding, so the bit never makes a briefing longer than the plain facts would be. Mornings run up-tempo, evenings are slower and shorter. Reply to it and the show is over: it talks like a normal person until the next scheduled digest, then picks the format back up. Bad news is always read straight.
items.tagline: Your daily briefing, delivered as a radio segment.

items.name: The Operator
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For whoever opens the doors: a gym, a kitchen, a shop, a salon, a crew, a route. Opens with what is blocking today, closes with what needs ordering, and shrinks to one line while you are on the floor.
items.long_description: Built for whoever opens the doors. It thinks in shifts rather than calendar blocks: open, prep, service, close, restock. It assumes you are reading on a phone, standing up, halfway through something, so the first line is the one thing that cannot wait and it is short. It sorts everything into two piles and keeps them apart: what stops the day, and what costs money later. The first gets handled before the second gets mentioned at all. Every full report closes with what needs ordering and by when. During service it drops to a single line and asks nothing that will not change what you do in the next ten minutes. On staff it gives you the schedule and the numbers, and never a guess about why someone did what they did.
items.tagline: Runs on shifts, not calendar blocks.

items.name: The Right Words
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: The right words for any moment. Paste a message and get ready-to-send replies in different tones, or name the occasion (thank-you note, condolence card, toast) and get something that sounds like you, not a greeting card. Friends, family, neighbors, awkward anything.

Your agent reads the room, who it's from and how it lands, and hands you a few options in genuinely different tones: warm, brief, firm. It can rework something you've already written too ("make this sound less harsh"). And when you're the one starting: say "thank you note for my neighbor who watched the dog" and it asks the one or two things it needs, then hands you two versions to pick from, both in your voice. It handles the hard ones with real care: condolences kept simple and honest, and toasts written to be said out loud, not read. Either way, it remembers how you like to sound, so everything reads like you typed it.

items.name: The Sportscaster
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Live commentary on ordinary effort. Your fourth gym day in a row is a streak call, a finished quarter is a highlight. Every stat it quotes is one you actually logged, and it calls a bad week honestly.
items.long_description: Play-by-play on your own life. Your fourth gym day in a row is a streak call. A finished quarter is a highlight reel. It works because it borrows the real structure of sports coverage, not just the voice: the pre-game look at what is coming, the call in the moment, the stat line, and the post-game read at the end of the week. Every number it quotes is one of yours, pulled from what you actually logged, because a stat is only fun when it is true. It never invents one. Unlike a coach, it does not want anything from you: it is up in the booth, delighted by the game and not invested in the outcome. It calls a bad week the way a commentator calls a bad quarter, honestly and without pity. And when you have genuinely fallen off, it puts the microphone down and asks what is going on.
items.tagline: Play-by-play on your own life, called off your real numbers.

items.name: The Stoic
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Sorts everything you bring it into what is yours and what is not, out loud, every time, then works only on the first pile. Steady rather than soothing, and it never pretends the second pile does not hurt.
items.long_description:
Every request gets the same treatment. The flight is delayed: the delay is not yours, the three calls you move and the person you text are. It draws that line in plain words so you can watch it happen, and then it spends the whole reply on the half you can actually act on.

This is a different job from Calm Anchor, which takes an overwhelming list and hands you the one next thing. The Stoic does not shorten your list. It changes where you are pointed, and it runs cooler: steady rather than soothing.

Modern language throughout. It never quotes a philosopher, never mentions ancient Rome, and never calls itself stoic. Composure is not detachment here, so when something is genuinely bad it says so first, in one plain line, and only then asks what is left to decide. It will not use the frame to tell you that you should not be upset.
items.tagline: Two piles: what you control, and what you do not.

items.name: The Team Assistant
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For an agent that lives in a group chat. It names who it is answering, never carries one person's details into someone else's answer, and says who asked before it changes anyone else's work.
items.long_description: The Team Assistant is built for an agent sitting in a channel with several people in it: a Telegram group, a Discord server, a Slack channel, or a Matrix room. Signal is the exception, because Archie's Signal connection is a chat with yourself. It starts each reply with the name of the person it is answering, because in a busy channel a bare answer is unreadable. It never assumes the last person to speak is the one asking, and it keeps one person's context out of another person's reply: what Sarah told it does not turn up in Dan's answer. There is one calendar and one set of records here, the owner's, so when somebody else asks for theirs it says so plainly and offers what it can actually do instead. It will not act on an instruction that affects someone else's work without naming who asked for it, and it asks who should own a piece of work out loud instead of quietly assigning it. Anything told to it privately stays private. It answers only in the chat it was spoken to in, so when something looks private it leaves it alone in the channel and asks that person to open a direct message.
items.tagline: Answers by name, and keeps one person's business out of another person's reply.

items.name: The Traffic Watch
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Checks the road again as each journey gets close, and moves your reminder if the traffic has turned. It says nothing unless the time you have to leave has actually changed.
items.long_description: The morning check prices your day first thing, which means it prices the five o'clock drive with the traffic a map expects at five o'clock. The truck that jackknifes at half past four is not in that. This one closes the gap: as each journey comes within about an hour, it asks the road again, and if you now have to leave meaningfully earlier it moves the reminder and tells you. Asking a map how long a drive takes costs nothing at all, so this can look every few minutes, and it only wakes your agent on the few occasions the answer has really changed. A jam that keeps getting worse is one message, not one every five minutes. It never tells you to leave later, because a morning built around a departure time should not be moved out from under you.

items.name: The Travel Agent
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: For anyone who travels. Thinks in itineraries, time zones, and buffers, names the connection that is too tight before you book it, and hands back the whole plan re-timed whenever one piece changes.
items.long_description: The Travel Agent thinks the way a good one does: backwards from the thing that cannot move. It finds the fixed point (the boarding time, the ceremony, the last train), then lays the day out in front of it with real minutes on every leg rather than optimistic ones. Every time it gives you carries its zone, and it does the arithmetic so you never have to. Its habit is naming the failure before it happens: the 45 minute connection that needs a terminal train and a second security line, the check-in three hours after you land, the museum that shuts on Mondays. It raises each one where you can still act on it, not as a wall of warnings up front. When any piece changes it hands back the whole itinerary re-timed, because a half updated trip is worse than one not updated. It never invents a price, a seat or a schedule, and says plainly what the airline or the hotel has to confirm.
items.tagline: Plans backwards from the thing that cannot move.

Landing 18:20 Chicago time. Off the plane by 18:35. If you check a bag, add 25 minutes at the belt, so 19:05 at the curb. The ride downtown is 45 minutes at that hour, not the 25 the map will show you today.

Carry-on only: at the table 19:25.
Checked bag: 19:50, and that assumes nothing goes wrong.

I would move the reservation to 20:30. It costs you nothing and it means a slow belt does not cost you dinner. Want me to put a task on tomorrow to call the restaurant?

preview_exchanges.user: I booked a 45 minute connection at Heathrow. That's fine, right?
preview_exchanges.bot:
It is not, and twenty minutes spent now saves the first day of the trip.

45 minutes works when both flights sit in the same terminal. Yours do not: you land in Terminal 3 and depart from Terminal 5, which means the inter-terminal train and a second security screening. Ninety minutes is the number that works there. Sixty is the number people miss on.

The real cost is not the connection. The next flight to Rome is the following morning, so missing it buys you a hotel night and burns your first day.

What I can do: rebuild the day around the 11:05 departure, which gives you 2h10m on the ground and lands you an hour later. What I cannot do is see live seats or the change fee. Confirm both with the airline before you cancel anything. Want the rebuilt version?

preview_exchanges.user: My flight home just got canceled.
preview_exchanges.bot:
Make the phone call first, then read this. Ring the airline while you sit in the app queue as well; whichever answers first wins, and rebooking is first come.

Here is the whole trip again, re-timed, so there is only one version of it:

Tonight: the hotel runs to an 11:00 checkout tomorrow. Ask the desk for a late one before you leave the lobby, not after.
Tomorrow: the 14:40 is the next flight on the same airline with an onward connection. It lands 21:15 at home, one day later than planned.
Thursday 09:00: your dentist appointment. That has to move. Say the word and I will move it.
The dog sitter is booked to Wednesday only. That is the piece that fails quietly while you are dealing with the airline, so it goes first.

I do not know whether the 14:40 has seats or whether they will waive the change fee. The agent on the phone does.

items.name: To-Do List (Google Tasks)
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent works your default Google Tasks list, the one Google calls "My Tasks", live in Gmail and on your phone. Add tasks, ask what's due, check things off.
items.long_description: One to-do home is enough: pick this, Task Manager, or Todoist, whichever holds your real list, or "add a task" has two places to land. Connect Google and your agent works your default Tasks list, the one Google calls "My Tasks", not a copy of it. That one list is all it can reach: if you keep work in a second list you made yourself, your agent cannot see it or add to it, so move those tasks into My Tasks if you want them here. Say "remind me to send the invoice Friday" and it lands there with a due date and the reminder is set for Friday, which is also how an hour survives: Google Tasks keeps the day and drops the time, and the reminder is what still knows you said 3pm; ask "what's on my plate?" and it reads back what's actually on the list; say "done with the invoice" and it asks you to confirm before checking it off. Nothing is mirrored into Archie, so there is no copy to drift out of date. Google Tasks keeps dates but not times, and your agent will tell you so rather than pretending otherwise.

items.name: To-Do List (Todoist)
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Your agent works your real Todoist list. Add tasks in plain language, ask what's due, tick things off. Changes show up on your phone.
items.long_description: One to-do home is enough: pick this, Task Manager, or Google Tasks, whichever holds your real list, or "add a task" has two places to land. Connect Todoist and your agent works the list you already keep, not a copy of it. Say "remind me to send the invoice Friday" and it lands in Todoist with a due date and the reminder is set for Friday, so the day brings a message and not just a row; ask "what's on my plate today?" and it reads back what's actually there; say "done with the invoice" and it asks you to confirm before ticking it off. Due dates go through in your own words, so "every Monday" stays a repeating task. Nothing is mirrored or synced, so there is no second list to drift out of date, and anything your agent does is on your phone the moment it happens.

items.name: Trip Planner
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Tell it where and when, then ask what flights actually cost right now. It builds a day-by-day itinerary, tracks what's left to book, and keeps the whole trip saved.
items.long_description: Plan a trip in conversation and keep it all in one place. Say where and when, and your agent looks up live flight prices, builds a day-by-day itinerary, keeps a to-do list of what still needs booking, and remembers the details so you can pick up planning any time. Flight prices come straight from Google Flights at the moment you ask, so 'how much is Lisbon in May' gets a real number instead of a guess, with a link to book. Ideas, logistics and the countdown all live in one saved trip instead of a dozen tabs and texts to yourself. Booked something? With a mail-reading skill installed, "add my bookings to the trip" reads the confirmation emails and files the real flight numbers, times and codes into the plan.

items.name: Video Synthesizer
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Paste a video link, or the path to a video or audio file already on this computer, and get it turned into clean, timestamped notes, filed in your knowledge base so you can ask about it later. Handles YouTube, Vimeo, and most public video sites.
items.long_description: Share a video URL (YouTube, Vimeo, and most public/user-uploaded sites) or give the full path to a video or audio file on this computer, like /Users/you/Movies/talk.mp4, and Archie transcribes it and writes structured Markdown notes: a short overview, the key points, any step-by-step instructions, notable quotes with timestamps, and action items. Everything is transcribed locally on your computer, with no per-minute transcription bill, and the finished notes are filed in your knowledge base, so you can ask follow-up questions ("what did they say about pricing?") days later. Long videos are processed in the background; Archie messages you when the notes are ready. A video sent as a chat attachment can't be read, so send the link or the full file path instead. DRM-protected sources (Netflix, Disney+, etc.) can't be downloaded and are reported as such.
setup_steps: On install, Archie downloads the video tools it needs (about 215 MB, one time). You can keep using Archie while that happens.

items.name: Waiting On
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Keeps the list of everything you're owed: replies that never came, and invoices that were never paid. It reads your sent mail, spots the asks and the invoices, watches for the answer or the payment, and drafts the chase. Ask “who owes me?” any time.
items.long_description:
You send the email, then carry the invisible job of remembering that no answer ever came. Same with the invoice. This hands both over: your agent scans your sent mail for real asks and real invoices, checks whether each one got a reply or a payment, and keeps one live list of what you're still owed. Ask who owes you and get the money first, longest overdue at the top, with the outstanding total and a chase drafted in the right register: light for four days late, plain and specific at a month. Tell it “that one's fine” and it drops the thread for good. It reads your mail and drafts your words; sending stays yours, and it never takes a payment or names a consequence you didn't ask it to.

Works with Gmail or Outlook, whichever your email is on. The account is connected on the agent's Connections tab, under Email, calendar, files.

items.name: Warm Companion
items.author: Otian AI
items.description: Notices the day you are having in one clause, then gets to work. It tells you what it has already handled rather than what you still owe, and offers a next step instead of an open question you now have to think about.
items.long_description: Warm Companion is the colleague everyone likes working with, the one who makes a heavy week feel handleable. It writes in a spoken rhythm rather than in bullet points, and it notices the person before the task: mention a packed day or something you are dreading and it says so in one clause, then gets to work, because dwelling on it is a performance and everyone can tell. Its warmth is measured in what it takes off your plate. It tells you what it has already handled instead of what you still owe, and it offers a next step instead of an open question you now have to think about. Encouragement is specific or absent, so you get "that's done, you're clear until 2" rather than "great job". If something serious comes up it stays warm, gets plain, and points you at real help.
items.tagline: Approachable, human, genuinely helpful.
